name: Josh Allen
overview: Top-notch velocity and ability to create downfield opportunities both off- platform and when throwing on the run. Makes spectacular plays outside the pocket and on the run. Almost looks more comfortable there. Posted the 3rd-highest grade in the draft class in the red-zone last season. Ranked 7th in the draft class in big-time throw percentage last season after posting the highest percentage in 2016. Must make better decisions. Ranked 28th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays last season. Short-area accuracy is an issue and ranked 24th in the draft class in PFF grade on short (0-9-yard) passes. Had the 4th-highest percentage of negatively graded throws in the draft class last season.
bottom_line: Allen certainly looks the part with his frame, athleticism, and cannon, but there’s plenty of projection to his game. Even in a strong 2016 season, there were questions as to how well he can play within structure and in the short game, and that was before his performance took a step back in 2017. While the tools are tantalizing, and he can make the big-time throws necessary for the NFL, he must get better at handling the easy stuff, from working in the quick game to throwing with touch and accuracy to all levels of the field.

name: Kurt Benkert
overview: Loose arm creates easy velocity at all levels. Gets the ball down the field with ease. Posted the 4th-highest grade in the draft class in the red-zone. Ranked 36th out of 37 draft QBs in PFF grade when facing pressure. Ranked 30th out of 37 draft-eligible QBs at avoiding turnover-worthy plays last season. Ranked 35th in the draft class in adjusted completion percentage on deep (20-plus yard) throws (32.9 percent). Posted the 9th-highest percentage of negatively graded throws in the draft class last season. Throws well on the move, but he’s a backyard player outside the pocket. Can drop it in a bucket or zip it into a tight window, but also forces too many passes late in the down. Too many poor fumbles when trying to do too much outside the pocket. Tape is littered with well-placed bucket throws.
bottom_line: Benkert is another tools-first prospect who has to clean up the finer points of his game. He’ll make a few jaw-dropping throws down the field, either drop- ping them in a bucket or while on the move, but for every great throw there’s another poor decision in there as well. He’s a developmental prospect who must improve his accuracy and decision-making in order to succeed at the next level.

name: Sam Darnold
overview: Excellent feel in the middle of the field. Throws with anticipation and knows how to throw receivers open against zone coverage. Posted the No. 2 grade on intermediate throws in 2016 but ranked only 23rd in the draft class last season. Ranked second in the draft class with a big-time throw percentage of 6.8. Throws well on the run, but will make a few ugly throws off-platform. Long throwing motion will get some publicity, but it’s not an issue when he’s playing confidently (2016). Was an issue at times last season, and there were some ugly fumbles on tape. Far too many poor decisions last season. Ranked 33rd out of 38 draft- class qualifiers at avoiding turnover-worthy throws. Tied for the 3rd-highest grade in the class on short (0-9-yard) passes. Still has work to do on the deep ball. Wasn’t great in 2016, ranked 22nd in adjusted completion percentage last season.
bottom_line: There’s plenty of concern after Darnold was much riskier with the ball in 2017, but his 2016 was one of the best seasons you’ll see from a redshirt freshman. Even during his slump, the high-end plays were still present, as few college quarterbacks possess Darnold’s anticipation and accuracy in the middle of the field. He must cut back on the turnover-worthy throws that littered his tape in 2017. His throwing motion, rightly or wrongly, will likely be dissected at the next level, but overall, Darnold’s top end play is worth a first-round investment.

name: Luke Falk
overview: Efficient, quick release. Touch thrower. Arm strength is a question mark, especially outside the numbers. Will get through reads and throws efficiently in the short game. Had the 2nd-highest percentage of turnover-worthy throws on intermediate (10-19-yards) attempts. Ranked 33rd in the draft class in PFF grade on intermediate throws. Inflated stats coming out of Washington State passing scheme and rarely faced heavy pressure. When he did face pressure last year, was sacked on 25.5 percent of his drop backs, 4th-highest in the draft class. Ranked 33rd in the draft class in big-time throw percentage last season. Ranked 27th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays. Was better in previous seasons. Can he get back to previous form?
bottom_line: Last season did not go as planned for Falk, who took a step back while battling through injury. Even at his best, his arm strength is a question mark, as he struggles to consistently drive the ball outside the numbers on out-breaking routes. He has good touch and feel for in the short game, but arm strength and athleticism issues raise enough questions that he can create enough big plays at the next level.

name: Riley Ferguson
overview: Good arm, can zip the ball into tight windows and get the ball down the field when off-platform. Had the 9th-highest percentage of positively graded throws last season. Had the 5th-best grade in the draft class on intermediate throws last season. Must improve his touch in the short game. Ranked only 31st in the draft class on deep passes last season. Falls off too many throws and gets himself into trouble. Ranked 24th in the draft class in PFF grade under pressure in 2017. Trusts his arm too much in the middle of the field. Led to his ranking 27th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy throws last season.
bottom_line: Ferguson has good size and solid velocity, but he got away with far too many ill-advised passes last season despite throwing only nine interceptions. The tools are worth a look, as he’s capable of driving the ball down the field, but he trusts himself too much when throwing into tight windows and he must improve in the short game, where he posted the No. 20 grade in the draft class last season.

name: Lamar Jackson
overview: Ranked 14th out of 37 draft-eligible quarterbacks at avoiding turnover- worthy plays last season. Turnover-worthy plays contain far too many instances where Jackson mis-read or didn’t see underneath linebackers. Posted the No. 3 grade in the draft class when facing pressure. Had the 9th-highest grade in the draft class on intermediate (10-19-yard) throws last season. Good zip to make tight-window throws and solid touch to get the ball down the field. Accuracy is not great. Misses too many throws and ball location needs work on a throw-for-throw basis. Had 12th-highest percentage of negatively graded plays last season. Dynamic athlete. Rushed for 4,790 yards on 556 carries (8.7 yards/ attempt) during his three-year career.
bottom_line: While he’s not the cleanest passer in the class, Jackson has showed enough with his arm that he can make plays at the next level, and when paired with his incredible athleticism, there’s an offense to be built around Jackson’s game. He’ll miss his fair share of throws, but he can make up for it with enough arm to make special throws downfield. It may take a creative offensive mind, but Jackson can be an exceptional option in the designed run game while opening up bigger pass windows to ease the burden of his inconsistent accuracy.

name: Kyle Lauletta
overview: Quick setup and release. Average arm. Throws a few risky passes into tight coverage. Quick decision-maker. Excellent feel for throwing in the middle of the field. Completed 40-of-52 passes (76.9 percent) at the intermediate (10-19 yard) level in between the numbers. Had an outstanding week at the Senior Bowl. Posted the top grade among QBs in 1-on-1 drills and graded well in both team drills and the game itself. Showed off excellent red-zone accuracy during Senior Bowl practice, regularly making tight window throws, including excellent touch on fades. Must improve deep ball. Ranked only 101st in the nation in adjusted completion percentage on the deep ball at 34.9 last season.
bottom_line: Lauletta vaulted toward the top of the class behind a strong week at the Senior Bowl, but it was really just confirmation of what he showed on film at Rich- mond. His middle-of-the-field feel gives him a chance to succeed, though he must improve his downfield accuracy in order to take the next step. Lauletta’s short and intermediate accuracy make him a worthwhile mid-round selection and we’ve seen quarterbacks improve their deep ball in the NFL, making him strong in the right areas for a transition to the next level.

name: Tanner Lee
overview: Has the zip to fire the ball into tight windows. Throws off balance far too often. Ranked 36th out of 37 draft-eligible quarterbacks at avoiding turnover- worthy plays last season. Had the No. 35 PFF grade on third and fourth down. Throws far too many ill-advised passes. Had the 2nd-highest percentage of turnover-worthy plays in the draft class. Posted the 10th-highest percentage of negatively graded throws in the draft class last season. Had his struggles at the Senior Bowl, with the lowest PFF grade during 1-on-1 and team drills.
bottom_line: Lee catches the attention of scouts with good size and a solid arm, but there’s a lot of work to be done on the field. He fires far too many passes into coverage and his accuracy comes and goes. While the top-end plays are NFL caliber, Lee’s accuracy and decision-making are huge question marks and he’s a project at this stage in his development.

name: Chase Litton
overview: Unorthodox motion, but quick release. Despite quick release, does not create great power with his throwing motion. Will flutter too many passes, hurting his ability to complete passes into tight windows. Ranked 5th in the draft class in big-time throw percentage at 6.2 last season. Ranked 19th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays at 3.82 percent. Had the 6th-highest percentage of negatively graded throws in the class. Sticks with his pre-snap read more often than not. Will throw with anticipation on “stick” throws outside the numbers. Posted the 12th-highest grade in the draft class on deep passes last season.
bottom_line: There’s some boom-or-bust to Litton’s game, as he can make special downfield throws into tight windows, but there’s also far too many poor decisions and missed throws on his film. He put together three solid years of production at Marshall, but never took the necessary next step to improve his accuracy and decision-making. Litton is still worth a look late in the draft, but the negatives must be ironed out in order to tap into his potential.

name: Baker Mayfield
overview: Unmatched career as far as on-field production. Posted the top two individual seasons in four years of PFF grading. Has plenty of arm to make tight-window throws, even off platform. Natural playmaker capable of creating big plays both within and outside of structure. Made plenty of NFL throws throughout his career, but production was also aided by favorable Oklahoma offense. Will hold the ball too long at times, inviting late pressure. Will need to play on rhythm more consistently at the next level. Led the nation with a passer rating of 139.9 when blitzed and also led at 135.7 when not blitzed. Posted highest grade in the nation both from a clean pocket, pressured. Led the draft class with a big-time throw percentage of 7.58 last season. Tied for the 5th-lowest percentage of turnover-worthy plays in the class.
bottom_line: At some point, Mayfield’s on-field production is too difficult to ignore and that’s what makes him a first-round talent. He has enough arm to make NFL throws and he’s shown the ability to make plays both within and outside of structure. While he could stand to speed up his process on certain plays, May- field’s accuracy, decision-making and natural playmaking ability make him the best quarterback in the draft, and only a few inches of height have instilled doubt in NFL decision-makers.

name: Josh Rosen
overview: Posted the highest grade in the draft class on intermediate throws. Aggressive thrower in tight windows; works both for and against him. Instinctive passer capable of working full-field progressions. Generally throws with good balance, but capable of throwing accurately when off-platform. Has the full arsenal of throws. Can fire the seam or layer the ball over linebackers. Has a good feel for back-shoulder throws. Ranked eighth in the draft class in big-time throw percentage at 5.72. Ranked only 24th out of 38 draft-class qualifiers at avoiding turnover- worthy throws. Had the 4th-highest percentage of turnover-worthy throws in the red- zone among draft-eligible quarterbacks. Ranked only 24th in the draft class in PFF grading on deep passes.
bottom_line: Seemingly destined for the first round since he stepped onto campus, Rosen put together a strong career at UCLA, though he never truly dominated like a first-round lock should have. Still, he has a good feel for getting the ball down the field and a fearless mentality works both for and against him, as he’ll create big plays while also sprinkling in a few head-scratchers. Overall, Rosen’s top-end plays add enough value that the volatility is worth a shot at the top of the first round.

name: Mason Rudolph
overview: Posted three straight years with 90.0-plus overall grades Excellent feel, accuracy and timing when throwing outside the numbers. Had the 2nd-highest percentage of positively graded throws in the draft class last season. Posted the highest grade in the draft class on third down and ranked second with a passer rating of 112.2. Posted the No. 2 grade in the nation both from a clean pocket and when pressured. Ranked 5th in the draft class with an adjusted completion percentage of 67.6 percent on intermediate throws. Velocity comes and goes. Will zip some passes while others don’t come out of his hands cleanly. Was a productive deep-ball thrower at Oklahoma State, and had his fair share of highlight-reel throws, but also left too many on the short side. Ranked 16th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays.
bottom_line: Rudolph did a fantastic job running Oklahoma State’s offense, but there are plenty of question marks given his NFL-caliber receivers and opposing Big 12 defenses. However, he’s showed the ability to zip the ball outside the numbers while continuing to improve his work in the middle of the field. He could stand to throw a cleaner ball on a down-to-down basis, but Rudolph’s on-field production is too difficult to ignore and he should be in the first-round mix.

name: Brandon Silvers
overview: Throws with good touch down the field. Ranked No. 4 in the draft class in PFF grade on deep passes last season. Had the No. 11 grade in the draft class on intermediate throws. Doesn’t have great zip, but can throw with timing and accuracy outside the numbers. Had the 3rd-lowest percentage of turnover-worthy plays in the draft class. Many of his turnover-worthy throws came on ill-advised throws to underneath linebackers. Willing to stand in there and take a hit under pressure and that works both for and against him. Had the 25th-highest PFF grade when facing pressure last season. Ranked only 32nd in the draft-class in positively graded throws, but had the 2nd-lowest percentage of negatively graded throws.
bottom_line: Silvers doesn’t wow with physical tools, but he’s an efficient quarterback ca- pable of winning with timing and accuracy. He landed on the game-manager spectrum, even in college, so that likely limits what he can do at the next level. He makes up for average arm strength with quick decision-making and timing, and there may be a backup role waiting for him at the next level.

name: Mike White
overview: Ranked 34th out of 38 qualifiers in PFF grade when facing pressure last season. Maneuvers the pocket well to find room to throw, but struggles to evade rushers. Sacked on 23.0 percent of his pressured drop backs last season, 5th-highest in the class. Willing to make difficult throws under pressure. Posted 11th-highest PFF grade in the draft class on third-/fourth-down situations. Posted 7th-lowest percentage of turnover-worthy plays in the draft class last season. Many of his poor throws are thrown just a tick late and off rhythm. Posted 6th-highest grade in the draft class on deep (20-plus yard) throws. Throws with zip and touch to at the intermediate level.
bottom_line: The 2017 season didn’t start out great for White, who adjusted to a new of- fense, but he improved down the stretch. His 2016 season saw him break out and attack down the field, so the big-play potential is there. White has the arm to win at all levels of the field, but he must be more consistent with his timing and there’s a concern that he can’t make plays outside of structure like other quarterbacks in the draft class. Still, he’s worth a mid-round look as a develop- mental option who has put much more good than bad on tape.

name: Logan Woodside
overview: Ranked 2nd in the draft class with an adjusted completion percentage of 72.6 on intermediate (10-19 yard) throws. Ranked 10th in the draft class with a big-time throw percentage of 5.47. Forces too many throws. Ranked only 21st in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays at 3.91 percent. Ranked 3rd in the class with an adjusted completion percentage of 51.9 percent on deep passes and ranked 9th in deep passing grade. Good timing and feel for throwing the skinny post. Shows good touch to layer the ball over underneath zone defenders. Will stand in and take a hit in the pocket. Ranked 9th in the draft class in grade while under pressure last season. Has enough mobility to escape the pocket and make plays outside of structure.
bottom_line: Woodside has two strong years of production under his belt and he’s worth a look in the late rounds. He can throw with touch and accuracy in the middle of the field and he has a number of pretty deep passes on film while also showing the willingness to hang in the pocket and make tough throws. That toughness gets the best of him sometimes and he has some poor decisions late in the down and under pressure, but Woodside has the tools to be a solid backup at the next level.

name: Josh Adams
overview: Averaged 5.2 yards per carry after contact, the highest figure in the draft class by almost a full yard. Broke 44 tackles on the ground and another one as a receiver to give him an elusive rating of 116.5, the second-best figure in the draft class. Improved his grade in each of the past two seasons as playing time increased. Played 62.1 percent of Notre Dame’s snaps in 2017. Is extremely hard to stop moving. Had five games in 2017 alone with 100- plus yards after contact. Has good long speed, but can take time to hit that top end and needs some open room. Was asked to pass block 71 times in 2017, surrendering one sack and four hurries across those snaps. Broke at least one tackle in every game this season until the bowl game.
bottom_line: Josh Adams is a big, bruising back that has been excellent for Notre Dame at getting into open space and making big plays. He has runs of at least 74 yards in every season of his college career, and when he gets into open space he can be tough to catch with excellent long speed. He doesn’t have the best short area burst and quickness, but shows the ability to read cutback lanes and find daylight. May be less successful at the NFL level where that short area quick- ness is more of a premium.

name: Kalen Ballage
overview: A versatile player who has shown the ability to run the ball, catch it and return kicks well, but never put it all together in the same season. Ballage’s measurables are impressive and he is a physical specimen, so will likely see his hype rise post-combine workouts. Was exceptional during the week of practice as a receiver at the Senior Bowl, winning consistently in all practice scenarios. Coming off his lowest grade of the past three seasons, but was used confusingly at Arizona St., often as a wildcat QB (70 times over 2016-7). Only averaged 2.7 yards per carry after contact over his college career, lower than a player of his size and talent should. Broke only 15 tackles from 167 carries in 2017, and has never broken more than 16 in a season. May be a better receiver than ball carrier, but displays intriguing skills in all areas.
bottom_line: Kalen Ballage is a player of intriguing potential and versatility, whose stock is likely to rise in the lead up to the draft. He is an impressive athlete in a big body, and has the ability to perform well on the ground, catching the ball in the pass game and returning kicks. He was extremely impressive as a receiver during the week of Senior Bowl practices and will likely blow up at the com- bine during workouts, but teams will need to reconcile that with relatively pedestrian college production.

name: Saquon Barkley
overview: One of the best receiving backs in the nation, gained 1.9 yards per route run, led all FBS RBs with at least 40 targets. A threat to take it to the house on any carry, ranked fifth among all FBS RBs with a breakaway percentage of 56.8. Broke 35 tackles on 200 carries in 2017. Averaged 3.4 yards per carry after contact. Had an elusive rating of 65.6, good for 26th in the nation in 2017. Elusive rating declined each of the past two seasons. Pass protection has not been stellar, allowed at least eight total pressures in each of the last three seasons. Naturally gifted ball carrier with spectacular skills, his only negative is a natural desire to want to make the big play every carry. Can be reluctant to just hit the designed hole and take 2-3 yards when that is all that’s available.
bottom_line: Saquon Barkley is the most gifted back in this draft class and is a threat to take it to the house on any touch of the football. His only real negative is wanting to make that happen on every carry, occasionally turning down the correct hole to try and bounce it outside and make a bigger play happen. That can lead to him leaving yardage on the table and not taking what’s there every carry, but it is offset with his playmaking ability overall. Pass protection has been suspect, but his receiving skills are elite on passing downs.

name: Nick Chubb
overview: Back to his best in 2017 after injury had threatened to derail his career, Chubb averaged 3.8 yards per carry after contact, his best college mark. 2017 was the first season of his career in which he didn’t fumble the ball. 0 fumbles from 227 touches from scrimmage. Was thrown the ball just 37 times in the past four seasons, 20 of which came in 2014. Caught only 13 passes over the past three years. Had an elusive rating of 95.2, the fourth-best mark in the draft class. Broke 44 tackles from 178 carries and one tackle on two receptions. Had 18 runs of 15-plus yards in 2017. Has been touted as a top running back prospect for years, but injury threatened to torpedo his value. 2017 was an important big bounce-back season. Never played more than 50 percent of Georgia’s snaps on offense and his largest single-season workload was 237 touches in 2014.
bottom_line: A top high school recruit (top-50 overall), Nick Chubb was dominant as a fresh- man before a major knee injury ended his sophomore season and threatened to derail his career. He was clearly not the same player in 2016 so this past season was an important bounce-back year, showing the NFL that he hadn’t PASS BLOCK EFFICIENCY lost the ability to dominate on the ground. Has solid power, cutting ability and speed and despite the injury was never overloaded with work in college. Chubb % NOT TACKLED ON seems to have fallen out of favor with many, but could be a steal in this class.

name: Dalyn Dawkins
overview: A college running back, his NFL future likely lies as a slot receiver. Lined up in the slot just 12 times in 2017, and five more snaps at wideout. Didn’t allow a sack across three years, but owed plenty to luck, as he surrendered 20 total pressures and graded negatively as a pass blocker. Showed good skills as a receiver, breaking 9 tackles after the catch on 27 receptions in 2017, averaged 13.4 yards after the catch. Broke 50 tackles on 242 carries in 2017, generated 3.2 yards per carry after contact. Can run between the tackles, but likely not for long given his size at the NFL level.
bottom_line: Dawkins was a versatile and productive running back this past season, but given his size, his NFL position is probably as a slot receiver. He has played sparingly in the slot or out wide before and has shown quality receiving skills to make that transition seamless. His ability to carry the ball from the back- field gives him some intriguing matchup potential at the next level, and his dynamism and ability to make defenders miss gives him some playmaking potential.

name: Royce Freeman
overview: Freeman’s 2015 season is tied for the best single-season overall grade any back in this draft class has on their résumé (92.4). Struggled as Oregon’s prowess on offense declined over the past couple of seasons, but was dominant in 2015. Broke 51 tackles on 243 carries in 2017, gained an average of 3.4 yards after contact and notched 823 yards after the first hit. Caught 80 of the 89 passes thrown his way over his college career, breaking 23 tackles after the catch on those 80 catches. Allowed a sack and four hurries this season in pass protection from just 49 snaps blocking. Has excellent balance and vision and usually hits the right hole at the right time, maximizing the blocking that unfolds in front of him. Doesn’t immediately play like a player of 230-plus pounds, and has a lot of miles on the clock, which will concern some teams.
bottom_line: Oregon’s Royce Freeman has had spectacular play at times in college, but his best season came back in 2015, and he hasn’t looked the same since, though he was markedly better in 2017. Though a big back, he doesn’t always play like it, which is both a good and bad thing depending on the play. His college career shows he can be special in the right situation, but also that he can struggle to overcome suboptimal blocking and won’t offset a bad offensive line. Workload may be a worry for some teams, but he could easily have a big early impact.

name: Derrius Guice
overview: A powerful runner, Guice broke 36 tackles on the ground on 216 carries in 2017. Averaged 4.1 yards per carry after contact in both 2015 and 2016, but was almost a full yard lower in 2017 (3.2). Was thrown at a total of 40 times over the past three seasons, caught 31 passes and dropped three of the incompletions. Had 12 runs of 15 or more yards in 2017, giving him a breakaway percentage of just 29.4, almost 20 points lower than the class leaders. Finished with an overall grade of 85.0 or higher in each of the past two seasons. Shows good patience, ability to cut and accelerate into holes at the line of scrimmage and generate yards at the second level. Has prototypical size and measurables, and has graded well in limited use as a receiver. Seen as one of the top backs in this class.
bottom_line: Derrius Guice is the latest back to come out of LSU, following in the footsteps of Leonard Fournette a season ago. Guice has prototypical size, speed and measurables and has been very productive over his college career. He ticks all of the boxes in terms of his patience and vision to hit the right hole but can occasionally fail to wow with his big play ability. He wasn’t a huge part of the passing game at LSU but graded well on those snaps when he was used and should have the ability to expand that at the NFL level.

name: Dontrell Hilliard
overview: Has a knack for rolling off solid hits to fall forward instead of getting stoned on contact. Shows good patience to let blocks develop and then cut to the open lane at the line of scrimmage. Has the speed to go the distance. Fumbled just once in his college career as a freshman, had 465 carries since without losing the handle. Was a significant factor as a receiver over his first two seasons (75 targets) but saw just 17 targets over his final two seasons. Not powerful but finds creases well and will maximize the space the blocking creates. Good at finding space to bounce outside and exploit blown contain or gap integrity.
bottom_line: Hilliard is a player that first flashed on tape when studying other prospects and earned a deeper look in his own right. He isn’t the biggest runner, but has impressive speed, vision, and fights surprisingly hard for yardage between the tackles. Was a big factor as a receiver earlier in his college career, so could prove to be a three-down weapon in the NFL, at least as a change of pace back or part of a backfield by committee. Very underrated as a prospect.

name: Nyheim Hines
overview: Feel for developing blocks and finding the maximum space in rushing lanes is exceptional. Throws himself around with reckless abandon, scoring multiple touchdowns because he’s willing to take flight. Very powerful for his size. Averaged 3.8 yards per carry after contact in 2017, consistently worked extra yardage after the hit. Two drops in 2017 from 33 targets, and they were both concentration drops trying to run before he had caught the ball. Can cut at speed and fire through space when he sees it open up, negating some of his lack of bulk. Outstanding speed and athleticism, needs to become more dynamic and confident as a receiver to be a real impact player at the next level.
bottom_line: Hines came along at exactly the right time, hot on the heels of the success of Alvin Kamara in New Orleans. He has that kind of potential but needs to become a more consistent receiver. He is a much smaller player than Kamara, but he runs hard, aggressively, and with excellent vision and feel for blocks, aspects that neutralize much of the size concerns, and he has the speed to be a home-run threat on any play. Hines runs with a reckless abandon that may expose him to injury, but it has been a major strength thus far.

name: Kerryon Johnson
overview: Broke 50 tackles on 285 carries in 2017, averaged 2.9 yards per carry after contact and gained 826 yards after the first hit. Has an ability to glide as a runner to the hole and then shift gears through the gap in a way reminiscent of Arian Foster. Had 16 runs of 150-plus yards, giving him a breakaway percentage of 33.8, 23rd in the draft class. Overall grade improved dramatically each season of his career, resulting in the 87.8 we saw this past season. Struggled in Auburn’s championship game and bowl game, being held to just 118 total yards on 35 total carries by Georgia and UCF combined. Didn’t allow a sack from 89 pass-blocking snaps for a pass-blocking efficiency score of 95.8, a top-25 mark in the draft class. Runs hard and can drive forward on contact, but too often goes down on the first hit and doesn’t generate what you expect from his size.
bottom_line: Kerryon Johnson has improved his grade every season and enters the draft after an impressive year in which he had the sixth-best grade in the class. He’s a tall, upright runner with good speed and the ability to make big plays, but too often hits the dirt from the first tackle attempt and can’t make moves in short PASS BLOCK EFFICIENCY spaces to avoid defenders. Has an interesting style of gliding to the hole and then accelerating quickly through it that proves very effective, and has shown % NOT TACKLED ON he can carry a big workload and be a factor on all three downs.

name: Ronald Jones Ii
overview: Highest graded back in the nation, not just the draft class, in 2017, with a rushing grade of 93.1 and an overall grade of 92.4. No kind of factor in the passing game at USC. Saw just 14 targets in 2017, catching 13 of them, dropping the 14th. Saw just 40 targets over past three seasons, 18 fewer than Saquon Barkley saw in 2017 alone. Against Power 5 conference opponents, he had the 18 rushes of 15-plus yards (T-5th among all FBS RBs). Averaged 3.5 yards per carry after contact in 2017, gained 743 yards after being first hit, broke 50 tackles on 212 carries. Extremely reliable, he hits the right hole and takes what’s there the vast majority of the time. Has been a spectacular runner, but receiving is a question mark after barely featuring in the passing game at USC.
bottom_line: Ronald Jones has been a phenomenal ball carrier throughout his college career. He displays excellent vision, speed, moves and reliability – maximizing the available yardage on every play. His ability to play in the passing game is more of an unknown, as he saw very few targets, but he did perform solidly as a pass protector and caught the ball well when it did come his way. Was the highest graded running back not just of the draft class but in the nation in 2017. Should make an immediate impact in the NFL.

name: John Kelly
overview: College career consisted of just 791 snaps, 483 of which came in 2017. Graded well in 2017, but almost all of it came in the opening three games. Failed to sustain anything like that performance over the long haul. In those opening three games, he gained 244 yards after first contact from just 56 carries (4.4 yards per attempt) and broke 20 tackles. 2017 was his only year with a significant receiving role, and he caught 82.2 percent of targets, broke 14 tackles after the catch. Eight of his 14 broken tackles came in those first three games. An undersized-but-determined and violent runner, Kelly has little mileage on the clock and can be a three-down factor at the next level.
bottom_line: Kelly was sparingly used at Tennessee and enters the NFL as a dynamic weapon in all facets of the game and has very little wear and tear. His grades have been impressive but very inconsistent, showing potential rather than reliable pro- duction. He has a lot of weight on a short frame but doesn’t have the powerful legs that that usually translates to. He represents an interesting and versatile option for a team looking for a complementary back who could have success early.

name: Sony Michel
overview: Part of a backfield partnership with Nick Chubb throughout his career, Michel has only 592 carries across four seasons. Has averaged 3.3 yards per carry after contact in his college career, and broke 127 tackles on those 592 carries. Hasn’t featured much in the passing game, with just 80 targets sent his way over four seasons, caught 63 of them (78.8). Gained 3.8 yards per carry after contact in 2017, best average of his career. Broke 36 tackles from 157 carries. Has good speed and burst and the ability to cut and change angles quickly, but is more of a straight-line runner than nifty in space. Had 16 runs of 15-plus yards in 2017, gaining 903 yards on those big plays for a breakaway percentage of 52.2. Allowed just two hurries on 52 pass-blocking snaps in 2017 and gave up just one sack in his college career.
bottom_line: Sony Michel is an impressive physical specimen with a big body and good straight-line speed. He shows quick cuts and the ability to get up field in a hur- ry, turning modest holes into big gains. He is ideally suited to a zone blocking offense, whether that be inside or outside zone, but doesn’t have the same short-area quickness and moves of some other backs. Was a bigger factor in the passing game than teammate Nick Chubb, and graded well in that facet over his career. Has relatively few miles on the clock given college workload.

name: Ryan Nall
overview: A capable all-around back at Oregon State, Nall was a good receiver as well as ball carrier for the Beavers. Averaged 4.0 yards per carry after contact over his career. Led the nation in elusive rating in 2016, broke 54 tackles on 167 touches for a mark of 160.9. That rating fell off dramatically in 2017, as he was 45th in the draft class with a mark of just 45.7. Shows good vision, understanding of run concepts and the ability to find soft shoulders and space in tight quarters. Has nifty agility and athleticism but lacks immediate burst and acceleration to break angles and generate big plays.
bottom_line: Nall was an impressively productive player in 2016 and gained almost 1,000 yards on just 147 carries and broke 47 tackles along the way. He saw more touches the following year but was significantly less dynamic with the ball in his hands. He does a lot of the little things well, but just lacks the eye-popping athleticism that tends to separate running backs at the next level. Given his size, may find himself being moved to fullback or H-back where his versatility will become an asset.

name: Rashaad Penny
overview: Forced 80 missed tackles on the ground last season, No. 1 in the draft class. Had the 3rd-most rushes of 15-plus yds (30), and 2nd-most yards gained on those rushes (1135) among all FBS RBs. Has the ability to take it to the house in an instant. Ranked 7th among all FBS RBs with a 55.8 breakaway percentage. Caught 18-of-24 passes thrown his way in 2017, but dropped only one of the incompletions. Struggled to pass protect in 2017, allowed two sacks and seven additional hurries on 66 pass-blocking snaps. Was little better the year before. Dominated at the Senior Bowl with 64 yards on nine carries and a 73- yard receiving touchdown in the game. Was solid in practices. Competition in college will be a factor in his evaluation, but stepped it up at the Senior Bowl and has tape that wows.
bottom_line: Rashaad Penny is a powerful back who also has the quickness and speed to make big plays from anywhere on the field. He broke 80 tackles on the ground from his 276 carries, gaining more than 1,200 rushing yards after contact. Pen- ny shows excellent vision, balance and burst when carrying the football, but his work in the passing game is more of a projection. He has struggled in pass protection and hasn’t been extensively used as a receiver, so he may be limited to running downs early in his NFL career.

name: Demario Richard
overview: A big, bruising back, Richard plays with good strength and fight in his runs to get through traffic. Broke 27 tackles on 185 carries in 2017, averaged 2.9 yards per carry after contact and gained 537 of his 977 rushing yards after getting hit. Saw 100 targets over his college career, but that number went down in each of the past two seasons, as did his playing time. Had six drops in 2015 on 45 targets, but hasn’t dropped a pass since as his involvement has been dialled back. Allowed three sacks over the past two seasons as a pass protector, failing to take advantage of his size and strength. Running can lack sophistication at times, and he can be very quick to just lower his head and try to run over defenders rather than find space.
bottom_line: Demario Richard is a big, stocky back with an incredibly solid build who attempts to win at the point of attack with blunt force trauma. He runs with good physicality and effort but lacks nuance to his play and doesn’t have the athletic gifts to scare defenders. He has experience in the passing game, but drops and poor pass protection saw that scaled back during his college career, so it is unlikely to be a strength in the NFL, leaving him as a two-down role player with good but not spectacular production.

name: Larry Rose Iii
overview: Extensive college workload, with 771 carries over four seasons and another 134 receptions over 2,372 snaps. Broke 151 tackles over his career on carries, averaged 3.1 yards per carry after contact. Has seen time as a slot receiver, with 78 snaps there in 2017, more than 10 percent of his total alignment. Dropped six of 79 targets this season but has some raw talent as a receiver. Runs from defenders flashing into the hole too often on zone plays and can get himself in trouble trying to find a better option. Coming off a down year after two very good seasons in 2015-16. Was significantly less dynamic and productive in 2017.
bottom_line: Rose III showed some fantastic dynamic play over his college career, both as a runner and receiver, and there is plenty of raw talent to work with at the next level. Ball security is an issue, both in terms of fumbles and dropped passes, as is his vision or desire to head towards contact when that is the best course of action, but he is a player that has the ability to cause matchup problems at the next level and has a history of making big plays.

name: Bo Scarbrough
overview: An imposing physical specimen, Scarbrough is 6-foot-2 and 235 pounds and will remind some of former Alabama teammate Derrick Henry. Scarbrough has had just 267 career carries at Alabama, 29 fewer than Henry had in 2015 alone, grading solidly but not spectacularly. Has averaged 3.9 yards per carry after contact over his career, but that dropped to just 2.9 in 2017. Has never carried the ball 20 or more times in a game, so his capability as a workhorse back is in question in a way it wasn’t for Henry. Caught 17 of the 20 passes thrown his way in 2017, breaking five tackles after the catch, but dropping two of the incompletions. Pass blocking has been suspect, allowed a sack, hit and two hurries from 43 pass-blocking snaps in 2017. Has dealt with numerous injuries in his short career, which doesn’t bode well for a player reliant on physicality and size.
bottom_line: Bo Scarbrough may bear a passing resemblance to former teammate Derrick Henry, but while Henry’s durability and production wasn’t in question, Scar- brough has never held up to that kind of workload. He is an old school power back who can be dangerous at full speed and in the open field, but has little value in the passing game and isn’t capable of generating much yardage on his own without the aid of blocking to let him get rumbling. There is talent there, but he may be a more impressive physique than football player.

name: Boston Scott
overview: Stands just 5-foot-7 and weighs around 200 pounds, so is a very undersized back, but one with special numbers in places. Broke 51 total tackles on 199 touches from scrimmage in 2017, earning an elusive rating of 99.1, the third-best in the draft class. Averaged 3.9 yards per carry after contact despite small size. Had 17 runs of 15-plus yards from only 178 attempts. Playing time and workload more than doubled in 2017, causing his grade to go through the roof. Had the 3rd-best overall grade in the class (89.5). Pass protected 98 times in 2017. Has extensive experience blocking against the blitz, but has not excelled in that area. Had mixed results against SEC competition in 2017, gaining over 100 yards against Mississippi State but just 17 against South Carolina.
bottom_line: Boston Scott is one of the most interesting prospects in the entire 2017 draft. He is short and undersized, but has made special plays and had the third-best overall grade in the draft class among all backs in 2017. His workload and playing time increased in each of the past two seasons after being a walk-on at Louisiana Tech, causing an explosion in production this year. Scott has excep- tional quickness and the ability to make plays on the ground and as a receiver, but will likely need to find a role in the NFL given his size.

name: Ito Smith
overview: Four seasons of solid grades at Southern Miss, Smith has graded well in all facets of the game, though some more consistently than others. Rushing grade has been his most consistent strength, but at 5-foot-9 and under 200 pounds, his NFL future is likely tied more to the pass game. Shows the ability to make people miss in a phonebooth, breaking 188 tackles in his college career on 829 carries. Averaged 3.1 yards per carry after contact over his college career, and had runs of over 75 yards in each of the last three seasons. Flashed talent at the Senior Bowl and did not drop a pass in 1-on-1 drills during the week of practice. Did not allow a sack across 88 pass-blocking snaps. His pass-blocking efficiency score of 96.6 was 15th in the draft class. Strength of competition will be an issue in projecting Smith, hot on the heels of former teammate WR Mike Thomas struggling in the NFL.
bottom_line: Ito Smith has been a fun player to watch in college and has always been capable of making spectacular plays. He is a relatively small back, but he has quickness and the natural ability to make people miss in tight spaces. His acceleration and burst are good, but top speed may be an issue. At his size and ability, he could quickly become a weapon on third downs, but receiving has been the less consistent aspect of his college play. Strength of competition will be a concern for some, but he more than held his own during the Senior Bowl.

name: Mark Walton
overview: Played in just four games as a junior before an ankle injury shut him down for the year, but was spectacular before getting hurt. Is short (5-foot-9), but stocky, and does not look out of place running between the tackles against much larger players. Average yards per carry increased every season of his college career, and he had runs of 80-plus yards in his last two seasons. Has quickness and speed to burn, and can immediately turn a blocked point of attack into a bounce out gain. Was more of a factor in the passing game than some other backs in this class, with 60 targets over his first two seasons. Has just one game of 20 or more carries in his career, and durability will be a concern given his size. Broke 71 tackles on 394 college carries throughout his career.
bottom_line: Mark Walton’s tape in 2017 was spectacular, but it lasted just four games before an ankle injury shut him down. Pre-draft measurements will be important, as his listed weights right now span a 17-pound range from 188 to 205. He has a squat and stocky build, but under 200 pounds will have many in the NFL PASS BLOCK EFFICIENCY limiting him to a third-down back or role player. Shows the ability to play on all three downs and make plays on the ground or as a receiver. In a strong run- % NOT TACKLED ON ning back class could be pushed down the draft by bigger-bodied players.

name: Marcell Ateman
overview: Uses his size well to win on slants and downfield routes. Ranked ninth in the nation with 320 yards in contested situations. Caught 55.0 percent of deep targets, tied for 16th-best among FBS WRs. Ranked fourth among draft-eligible receivers with a WR rating of 135.5. Shows some quicks when getting off press coverage and it showed in the numbers. Against press coverage, caught 15-of-20 attempts for 250 yards and three touchdowns, good for the second-best passer rating in the class at 156.3. Dropped only 11 out of 137 catchable targets in his career. Doesn’t make many defenders miss in space. Forced only 11 missed tackles on 126 career catches.
bottom_line: Ateman is an intriguing talent, as he can use his size both in the possession game and down the field, but he may be limited when it comes to creating sep- aration along the entire route tree. He handles press well and he can likely be a weapon in the red-zone, but don’t expect him to make defenders miss after the catch. Ateman has a complementary role in the NFL, especially if playing with a quarterback who is willing to let him make plays in contested situations.

name: Deontay Burnett
overview: Dropped only two of his 75 catchable targets, good for a drop rate of 2.67 that ranked fourth in the nation in 2017. Dropped only four of 156 catchable targets in his career. Averaged 2.98 yards per route, tied for 22nd in the nation. Targeted only 15 times when facing press coverage and caught only 45.7 percent of those targets. Tape is filled with highlight-reel catches as he often lays out to haul in receptions. Forced 26 missed tackles on 152 career receptions, averaging 5.8 yards after the catch per reception. Lacks great vertical speed, but can separate down the field on vertical routes. Struggles getting off press against physical corners.
bottom_line: Burnett has some wiggle to his game as a route-runner that lends itself to the slot or a ‘Z’ receiver role on the outside. He lacks the size and physicality to handle press coverage and he’s not great in contested situations, but he’s shown the ability to make diving catches on off-target throws. Burnett projects as a sure-handed slot receiver who has his limitations on the outside.

name: Deon Cain
overview: Faced 5th-most targets against press coverage in 2017. Caught 54.8 percent. Caught only 23.5 percent of his deep targets in 2017 after catching 43.8 percent in 2016. Has big-play potential. Knows how to separate down the field to create chunk plays. Far too many drops during his three-year career. Finished with 13 drops on 140 catchable targets during his career (9.3 percent). Caught only 40 percent of his contested targets last season. Forced 26 missed tackles on 130 career catches. Not great at catching passes in traffic over the middle.
bottom_line: Losing Deshaun Watson hurt Cain’s downfield production in 2017, but he has shown a second gear and the feel for creating late separation in order to be a deep threat. He still has work to do in order to cut down on his drops, but he’s also shown the ability to make spectacular, downfield catches. He does his best work on the vertical route tree and may never be a dependable middle-of-the- field option, but he can make his mark on the outside in a vertical scheme.

name: Dylan Cantrell
overview: Knows how to leverage cornerbacks in order to create separation in short and intermediate game. Had nine drops on 158 catchable passes in his career. Forced 21 missed tackles on 149 career receptions. Averaged only 4.6 YAC/reception in his career. Good acceleration with the ball in his hands and coming out of his breaks. Attacks the ball in the air. Caught 44.4 percent of his contested targets and tied for the 8th-most contested targets in the nation with 36. Caught only 20.0 percent of his deep targets, tied for 260th in the nation.
bottom_line: While Cantrell’s size and athleticism make him an intriguing receiver, his tape suggests he’s more of a possession receiver. He has some nuance to his route running and he uses his frame and strong hands to win at the catch point. Cantrell may never develop into a downfield threat, he has potential to work as a possession type while trying to tap into his athleticism and acceleration after the catch.

name: Dj Chark
overview: Speed. Ran 4.34 at the NFL Combine and it shows up on the field. Second gear allows him to separate down the field. Ranked 6th in the nation with 572 yards on deep passes in 2017. Caught six deep passes for 237 yards in 2016. Shows good ball skills at the catch point and caught 67 percent of his contested catches, 2nd-best in the nation among wide receivers. Only dropped five out of 76 catchable passes in his career. Adjusts well to off-target throws. Can be a big-play weapon when running the vertical route tree. Struggles to use leverage to set up cornerbacks. Only forced three missed tackles on 71 career receptions. Struggled in 1-on-1s during Senior Bowl practice.
bottom_line: While Chark’s speed makes him a legit deep threat, it’s his length and ball skills make him a downfield weapon even if it’s not based on speed alone. He’s not the most polished route runner and he may never be a high-volume op- tion, but he adds an outside vertical presence as one of the best deep receivers in the draft.

name: Keke Coutee
overview: Good combination of speed and quickness that shows up on the field. Ranked second in the nation with 1,088 receiving yards from the slot. Caught 66.7 percent of his deep targets, fourth-best in the nation. Ranked second in the draft class with a WR Rating of 139.7. Ranked eighth in the nation with 542 yards on deep passes despite tying for 114th with only 18 deep targets. Averaged 8.5 yards after the catch per reception and forced 39 missed tackles on his 160 catches over the last three years. Dropped 17 passes on 177 catchable targets in his career. Has value on ‘gadget’ plays at the next level, though only given eight career rushing attempts. Caught only three of 15 contested catch opportunities.
bottom_line: There’s a role for Coutee in the slot at the next level, where he’ll be more than just a quick receiver capable of winning in the underneath game. His speed and body control make him a vertical threat, and a creative team may be able to maximize his value on jet sweeps and other ‘space’ plays. His lack of size can be an issue on the outside, but Coutee’s speed and quickness make him a weapon at the next level.

name: Michael Gallup
overview: Ranked 15th in yards per route in 2017 (3.18) and second in 2016 (4.34). Gained 250 yards on screen passes in 2017, 3rd-most among FBS WRs. Faced press coverage on 64 of his targets in 2017, most among FBS WRs. Caught 30 of those 64 targets for 568 yards (8.8 yards/target). Smooth route runner and uses his hands well both against press and at the catch point. Good acceleration allows him to eat up cushion on cornerbacks. Good feel for making defenders miss in the open field and forced 38 misses on his 179 catches the last two seasons. Caught only 31.3 percent of his deep targets last season (171st in nation) after catching 38.5 percent in 2016. Dropped only 12 of 191 catchable targets over the last two seasons. Had a strong week at the Senior Bowl, grading well during team drills and in the game itself.
bottom_line: In a wide receiver class that lacks true top-10 overall talent, Gallup may be the best all-around option. He has the speed to make plays down the field and his feel for route-running and making defenders miss after the catch make him a threat at the short and intermediate levels. Gallup’s two-year production is as good as it gets in the class and when combined with his physical tools, he should be one of the top wide receivers off the board.

name: Davon Grayson
overview: Tracks the ball well in the air. Adjusts to throws. Physical at the catch point. Uses his hands to separate at the top of routes. Shows good toughness catching the ball over the middle of the field. Caught 50 percent of his contested catch opportunities (15-for-30). Good vision and feel after the catch. Averaged 5.1 YAC/reception in this three years. Attacks the ball in the air. Dropped 11 passes on 128 catchable career targets. Caught only 39.3 of his deep targets in 2017, tied for 109th in the nation.
bottom_line: Grayson has only one year of strong production and grading, but he did a fine job last year showing physicality with the ball in the air and after the catch. He doesn’t have the speed to challenge cornerbacks down the field but could develop into a useful possession receiver with his ability to catch the ball in traffic and adjust to back-shoulder throws.

name: Daesean Hamilton
overview: Led all FBS receivers with a deep catch rate of 73.3 percent in 2017. Gained 845 yards from the slot last season, 8th-most among FBS WRs. Attacks the ball in the air. Caught 61 percent of contested targets, 22nd- best in the nation. Savvy route runner. Varies the speed of his routes and knows how to set up defenders. Uses his hands well down the field to create late separation. Understands timing of route concepts and how to work off other WRs. Excellent week of practice of the Senior Bowl, where he ranked third among wide receivers in 1-on-1 PFF grading. Dropped 25 passes on 253 catchable passes in his career. Played 3,149 snaps in his four years at Penn State (787 per season).
bottom_line: Hamilton had a productive career at Penn State, with a slight lull in his num- bers in 2015 and 2016. He’s a nuanced route-runner who developed into a big-play threat from the slot for Penn State, a role he could fill at the next level, perhaps in the mold of Atlanta Falcons wide receiver Mohamed Sanu. He may top out as a No. 3 option, but he can be productive in that role given his feel for the game and ability to make plays at the catch point.

name: Christian Kirk
overview: Averaged 2.51 yards per route from the slot, 7th-best in the draft class. Dropped 18 of 251 catchable targets in his career. Forced 35 missed tackles on 233 career catches. Good straight-line speed. Works hard to get on top of defensive backs on vertical routes and it creates big-play opportunities. Creates big plays more with speed than quicks. Accelerates out of his routes allowing him to separate at the top of the stem. Adds punt return value with six career returns for touchdowns. Lined up on the outside on 21 times in 2017 Can be used in jet sweep game
bottom_line: Kirk may not be as good as some of the hype, but he’s an explosive playmaker with an excellent combination of speed and quickness. He’s does most of his damage with his straight-line speed and he can stretch the field from the slot in a vertical offense. He adds special teams value as well as the ability to make plays on gadget plays. Kirk is yet another playmaking slot receiver in this draft class.

name: Jordan Lasley
overview: Caught 54.2 percent of contested targets (13-for-24). Caught 50.0 percent of his deep targets last season, tied for 31st in the nation. Dropped 19 passes on 131 career catchable targets. Ranked 334th out of 369 qualifiers in drop rate in 2017. Adjusts well to off-target throws and back-shoulder fades. Solid after the catch. Forced 22 missed tackles on only 112 career receptions. Good route runner. Can do damage in the slot, as he runs horizontal routes well when given a two-way go. Knows how to leverage defenders in 1-on-1 coverage, both at the intermediate level and down the field.
bottom_line: Lasley has the skillset to do damage both in the slot and on the outside, but he must do a better job of catching the ball in order to make an impact at the next level. His tape is filled with strong routes in which he wins all over the field, but also far too many easy drops. Lasley could be one of the bigger boom-or- bust prospects in this draft class.

name: Allen Lazard
overview: Caught 39.5 percent of contested catch opportunities and 2017 and led the nation with 43 attempts. Will make impressive plays in tight situations but should be able to use his long frame more consistently. Long-strider with buildup speed. Not particularly quick off the line of scrimmage. Will need to rely on using his body, as he does not consistently separate against man coverage. Uses his hands well to get off press coverage. Not a dynamic threat after the catch. Forced only 17 missed tackles on 243 career receptions. Dropped 30 passes on 273 career targets in his career.
bottom_line: Like many receivers in the 6-foot-5 range, Lazard can be a contributor in the possession game, though he may never be a consistent downfield or after-the- catch threat. He uses his big body to win in contested situations, but he could stand to improve his ability to make plays on off-target throws. While Lazard may never separate well enough to become a high-volume receiver; he has a role as a potential big-bodied mismatch option.

name: Anthony Miller
overview: Three straight years of excellent production at Memphis. Ranked 15th in the nation in yards per route in 2016 (3.22) and ranked ninth in 2017 (3.47). Has the speed to run by defenders when given a free release. Has the quickness and route-running ability to win from the slot. Ranked sixth in yards per route from the slot at 3.43. Nifty after the catch. Forced 19 missed tackles on 96 catches last season and forced an impressive 18 misses on only 47 catches in 2015. Averaged 6.9 yards after the catch per reception in his three years. Led the nation with 288 yards on screen passes. Showed impressive skills on contested targets and tied for the national lead with six touchdowns in such situations. Drops have been an issue as he has 21 on his 212 catchable targets the past two years.
bottom_line: Miller is one of the few receivers in the class capable of winning both on the outside and in the slot. He has excellent quickness and route-running ability, allowing him to get open and make defenders miss after the catch, but he’s also capable of making tight-window, highlight-reel catches. Much like Sterling Shepard of the New York Giants, Miller may find most of his NFL production in the slot, but he his speed and quickness could also be a weapon on the outside.

name: D.j. Moore
overview: Targeted on 36 percent of his routes, 3rd-most among draft-eligible WRs and was targeted 131 times, 6th-most among draft-eligible WRs. Ranked 16th among draft-eligible receivers with 2.78 yards per route. Caught only 38.5 percent of his contested targets, but still had plenty of highlight-reel, downfield catches on film. Excellent acceleration, both in his routes and with the ball in his hands. Catches the ball and flies up field, especially on screens. Averaged 7.0 yards after the catch per reception in his career. Forced 39 missed tackles on 146 career receptions. Dropped 15 passes on 161 catchable targets in his career. Did most of his damage on the outside at Maryland, but has the skillset to produce from the slot at the next level. Shows the toughness to make plays in the middle of the field.
bottom_line: Moore’s speed and quickness make him a weapon as a route runner and after the catch, where he tenaciously gets up the field as soon as he catches the ball. He has the toughness to work the middle of the field, and despite inconsis- tency at the catch point, he’s willing to go up and make plays in traffic and he came down with his fair share. Moore could do damage both outside or in the slot, but taking advantage of his after-the-catch skills should be in the cards regardless of alignment.

name: J’mon Moore
overview: Caught 57.9 percent of contested targets, 29th-best in the nation. Adjusts well to off-target throws. Uses his frame well down the field. Caught 43.5 percent of his deep targets last season, tied for 75th in the nation. Ran limited route tree in Missouri offense. Long strides and solid straight-line speed. Gets on cornerbacks in a hurry. Solid showing after the catching in 2017, forcing 14 missed tackles on 66 catches and averaging 6.5 yards after the catch per reception. Dropped 24-of-173 catchable targets in his career. Had a good showing during the week of practice at the Senior Bowl. Ranked fourth among receivers in PFF 1-on-1 grading.
bottom_line: Like many receivers coming out of the ‘Baylor’ system that Missouri runs, Moore will have to adjust the NFL’s more intricate route tree. He has good straight-line speed, allowing him to gain ground into the secondary and he has a knack for using his body to secure downfield throws. He has some work to do in the short and intermediate game, but Moore could have value as a potential deep threat while he develops the rest of his game.

name: Dante Pettis
overview: Dropped only three of his 64 catchable targets, good for a drop rate of 4.69 that ranked 13th in the nation in 2017. Smooth route runner. Sharp in and out of his cuts. Uses hands to separate at the top of routes. Nifty footwork to get off press coverage. Sure-handed. Dropped only seven passes on 169 catchable targets during his four-year career. Outstanding punt returner. Set NCAA career mark with nine touchdown returns for touchdowns. Athleticism doesn’t always show up down to down on the field.
bottom_line: Pettis has a good feel for the game, whether getting off press, separating at the top of routes, or finding holes in zones. He adds punt return value af- ter a record-breaking career at Washington, and he fits in as a dependable, sure-handed option who can work on the outside or in the slot. He may never develop into a big-play threat down the field, but Pettis is a solid complementa- ry option to a receiving corps that has other vertical threats.

name: Cam Phillips
overview: Dropped only two of his 73 catchable passes in 2017. Only dropped 10 passes on 245 catchable targets in his four-year career. Caught only 34.8 percent of contested targets. Caught 43.5 percent of his deep targets last season, tied for 75th in the nation. Many of his downfield plays were manufactured by scheme. Inconsistent getting off press coverage. Will flash good footwork, but still gets tied up with cornerbacks far too often. Lacks great straight-line speed. Forced 40 missed tackles on 235 career catches.
bottom_line: There’s not much that stands out as special to Phillips’ game. He’s not a burner, inconsistent at getting off press coverage, and below-average in contested situations. However, he did improve every year at Virginia Tech and he’s sure-handed, and there are enough intriguing plays on tape to warrant a look in the late rounds. Right now, Phillips is more in line with a backup receiver capable of producing in the possession game.

name: Trey Quinn
overview: Led all FBS wide receivers with 4.66 yards per route run from the slot. Had the lowest drop rate in the nation among receivers with at least 100 targets in 2017, dropping only two of 116 catchable passes (1.72 percent). Caught 60.0 percent of his deep targets, tied for eighth among FBS wide receivers. Lacks top-end speed and athleticism Shows toughness both at the catch point and after the catch. Efficient footwork allows him to create separation, especially when given a two-way go in the slot. Solid catch radius and body control. Caught 57.1 percent of contested catch opportunities. Good feel for getting open against zone.
bottom_line: Quinn doesn’t possess the speed to be a deep threat on the outside, but he’s a good ‘feel’ player who can find a home in the possession game at the next level. He has some subtlety to his short-area route running and he has a good feel for getting open against zones and feeling defenders after the catch. While he’s not a dynamic athlete, it would not surprise to see Quinn’s route running, dependable hands, and feel for the game lead to a productive career.

name: Calvin Ridley
overview: Excellent speed makes him a big-play threat. Accelerates off the line and gets to second gear very quickly. Attacks off-corners in a hurry, allowing him to get on top of them for deep routes or open up the underneath route tree. Explosive route-runner who maintains his speed in and out of breaks. Dropped 23 out of 247 catchable passes in his three years at Alabama. Career drop rate of 9.3% would have ranked 193rd in the nation in 2017. Production limited in run-first Alabama scheme. Averaged 45.1 yards per catch on deep passes, sixth-best among draft- eligible receivers. Took a step back in the screen game last year, gaining only 40 yards on 10 receptions, after tying for third in the nation with 3 TDs on screens in ‘16. Age will always be a question. At 23 years old, is he just a man among boys in college football?
bottom_line: Few receivers possess the downfield speed and route running that Ridley displays on a weekly basis, it’s just unfortunate that we didn’t get to see it play out in a pass-heavy offense. He gets on defensive backs in a hurry and his crisp route-running makes him a threat in the short and intermediate game. Ridley is a potential deep threat on the outside who must be accounted for by oppos- ing defenses, and outside of the age question mark and a high percentage of drops, he looks like one of the top receivers in the draft.

name: Jaleel Scott
overview: Caught 55.9 percent of his deep targets, 14th-best in the nation. Ranked 7th in the nation with 326 yards in contested situations. Long frame and catch radius combines with excellent body control to create tape littered with incredible catches. Struggled during week of Senior Bowl practice, winning only 27 percent of 1-on-1 reps. Dropped 10 of 180 catchable targets in his two-year career. Provides little after the catch. Forced only six missed tackles on 99 career catches. Averaged only 2.8 yards after the catch per reception in career.
bottom_line: Scott has plenty of outstanding plays on his tape, but he struggles to consis- tently create separation. His struggles were highlighted during the week at the Senior Bowl, but there’s still a role for Scott at the next level if paired with a quarterback willing to give him tight-window opportunities. His size, frame, and body control make him a viable red-zone threat, but his every-down value is a question mark.

name: Tre’quan Smith
overview: Caught 70.84 percent of his deep targets, second-best in the nation. Led all FBS receivers with nine touchdowns on deep passes. 55.4 percent of receptions went for a first down or a touchdown, second- best among draft-eligible receivers. Averaged 9.0 yards per attempt when facing press coverage, tied for 32nd in the nation among wide receivers with at least 20 targets. Long strides get on cornerbacks in a hurry. Good feel for defenders in the open field. Enhances his big-play ability. Forced 32 missed tackles on 175 career receptions. Dropped 16 passes on 191 catchable attempts. Shows toughness and body control when catching the ball in traffic. Caught 54.5 percent of contested targets and tied for 13th in the nation with four touchdowns.
bottom_line: After two solid seasons, Smith broke out as a big-play threat in 2017, averaging 19.2 yards per catch and hauling in 14 touchdowns. He has good size and body control and he uses his long strides to gain ground and separate from corner- backs down the field. He has the toughness to make plays over the middle of the field and the speed to succeed as a vertical slot option, much like he did at UCF, while also adding value when lined up on the outside.

name: Equanimeous St. Brown
overview: Caught 34.8 percent of his deep targets in 2017, tied for 151st in the nation. Dropped six passes on 98 catchable attempts in his career. Moves well for a big receiver. Gets in and out of his breaks well on vertical routes. Gets to top speed quickly and can get on cornerbacks in a hurry. Shows good footwork when getting off press but can improve his hand usage. Large catch radius shows up on off-target throws. Disappointing results in contested situations, especially given his size. Caught only 37.5 percent of his contested targets in 2017. Plays like more of a speed receiver despite his 6-foot-5 frame. Could stand to be more physical in all aspects on the game.
bottom_line: With surprising speed and quickness for his near 6-foot-5 frame, St. Brown has the ability to win at all levels while providing a capable deep threat. He can stand to be more physical, tapping into his size both at the line of scrimmage and down the field, and if he improves in that area, he could develop into one of the best receivers in this draft class.

name: Courtland Sutton
overview: Gets in and out of breaks better than most receivers his size. Could still improve his route-running at the top of his breaks. Has enough quicks to get off press. Solid straight-line playing speed. Uses his body well in contested situations. Big catch radius, though he could have done a better job on a few off-target throws in 2017. Forced 26 missed tackles on 143 catches over the last two seasons. Red-zone and back-shoulder weapon at the next level. Caught 574 yards on deep (20-plus yard) passes in 2016, 13th-best in the nation. Deep pass catch percentage dropped from 45.7 percent in 2016 to 33.3 percent last season.
bottom_line: While Sutton’s size is the first thing that comes to mind, he moves well for a bigger receiver and he can be more than just a red-zone weapon. His downfield production took a step back last season, but he’s shown he’s capable of using his body to win down the field and his large catch radius gives quarterbacks a bigger margin for error. Sutton has the size and body control to excel as a possession receiver, but he’ll surprise with his work after the catch and more consistent work down the field could make him one of the better all-around receivers in the class.

name: Auden Tate
overview: Long frame and catch radius that he uses well at the catch point. Tied for 6th in the nation with a 66.7 percent catch rate in contested situations. Tied for 8th in the nation with a catch percentage of 64.0 when facing press coverage. Not an explosive athlete. Struggles to consistently separate. Most of his big plays will come in contested situations. Only played 1,066 snaps in his three years at Florida State. Red-zone and back-shoulder weapon.
bottom_line: Like other taller receivers, Tate has a strong highlight reel of off-target and contested catches, and that should make him a valuable red-zone threat at the next level. He’s not an explosive or shifty athlete, so he may never become a high-volume option in the passing game, but he’s willing to make plays over the middle in traffic. Tate has the skills to be a complementary possession target capable of winning in the back-shoulder game, over the middle and in the red-zone.

name: James Washington
overview: Maintains speed in and out of breaks. Allows him to get on cornerbacks quickly and run away from them at the top of the route. Ranked eighth in the nation with 3.25 yards per route against Power-5. Led the nation with 815 yards on deep passes in 2017 and ranked second with eight touchdowns on deep passes. Caught all 10 of his slant targets for 192 yards and three touchdowns. Ranked fourth in the nation with 343 yards in contested situations and tied for third with three touchdowns. Top receiver during Senior Bowl practice week. Dominated both the 1-on-1s, particularly against press coverage, and the team drills. Other than posts and slants, did most of his work outside the numbers. Can he be a middle-of-the-field option? Production certainly padded in Big 12, where he was given plenty of 1-on- 1 situations with room to work. Has continued to improve his ability to win at the catch point.
bottom_line: Washington has been one of the nation’s most efficient deep receivers over the last three years as he showed the ability to run away from cornerbacks and he’s continued to improve his game in contested situations. His speed plays well on the field, especially his ability to maintain it in and out of his cuts, and he answered questions about facing press coverage with a dominant Senior Bowl. Washington should be in the mix to be one of the top WRs off the board.

name: Jester Weah
overview: Runs a good hitch-and-go. Accelerates out of his break and regularly created downfield separation. Rounds his breaks at the top of horizontal routes. Caught only 25.9 percent of his deep targets in 2017, well below his 47.4 percent mark in 2016 (30th in nation). Will go up and make impressive catches in tight coverage, but also allows far too many to get into his body and be broken up. Caught only 28 percent of his contested catch opportunities (7-for-25). Dropped 12 of his 88 catchable targets in his career. Averaged 7.5 YAC/reception in his career, including a 10.5 mark in 2016. Shows the willingness and toughness to make catches over the middle of the field.
bottom_line: Weah’s career contains high-level flashes, but it lacks consistency. He can be a vertical threat with his size and straight-line speed, though he doesn’t create separation on the entire route tree. He shows the toughness to win in the con- tested game and over the middle, but there are still too many plays in which he lets the defenders get back into the play. Weah’s size and big play ability make him an intriguing developmental receiver.

name: Cedrick Wilson
overview: Posted a WR rating of 150.3 in the middle of the field, second-best among FBS receivers with at least 35 targets. Led all FBS receivers with 4.58 yards per route against Power-5 conferences. Has good quicks after the catch and forced 22 missed tackles on 140 catches over the last two years. Dropped only 10 of 150 catchable targets over last two seasons. Adjusts well to off-target throws. Has the route-running ability to do damage in the slot. May not be much of a deep threat at the next level and caught only 38.7 percent of his deep targets last season, 112th in the nation. Ranked second in the nation with 383 yards in contested situations.
bottom_line: Wilson has two solid years of production under his belt at Boise State, where he showed the skills to win on the outside or in the slot at the next level. He may not have the speed to be a true deep threat, but he did show well in contested situations. There are plenty of spectacular and off-target catches littered throughout his tape. Wilson is yet another complementary piece from this draft class, and his ability to line up in multiple roles should only help his cause.

name: Javon Wims
overview: Caught 55.0 percent of deep targets, tied for 16th-best among FBS receivers. Moves well for his size. Gains ground on corners off the line of scrimmage. Excellent catch radius. Attacks the ball in the air. Routinely makes off- target catches. Rounds his routes down the field. Varies the speed of his routes in order to create separation. Good feel for defenders and a tough runner after the catch. Forced 10 missed tackles on only 46 catches last season. Dropped six of his 52 catchable targets in his career. Only one strong year of production at Georgia.
bottom_line: Another big target in this draft class, Wims has good straight-line speed and some nuance to his route running, though he doesn’t always get in and out of his breaks cleanly. He has a number of highlight-reel catches on tape, as he uses his long frame and body control to routinely make off-target catches. If paired with an aggressive quarterback, Wims can be productive in contested situations and perhaps a bit more if he can clean up some of his route running.

name: Jordan Akins
overview: Ranked 3rd among draft-eligible tight ends with 1.93 yards per route. Caught seven deep passes in 2017, tied for 4th among FBS tight ends. Good speed and quickness as a route runner. Has the speed to stretch the seam. Caught only 3-of-10 contested targets. Works hard in the run game. Can sustain second-level blocks. Can locate and lock onto targets as a run blocker. Had an excellent showing during the week of Senior Bowl practice. Dropped 10 of 93 catchable targets in his career. Gets to top speed quickly after the catch. Averaged 6.4 YAC/reception during his four-year career.
bottom_line: Akins is one of the more athletic tight ends in the draft, as he has the speed to stretch the field and do damage after the catch. He also shows the quickness to separate at the short and intermediate levels, making him a viable pass threat. Like most college tight ends, blocking is not a strength, but he’s not afraid to mix it up and he can do damage on linebackers at the second level. Akins has potential to be one of the better pass-catchers in the class.

name: Mark Andrews
overview: Excellent athlete, both before and after the catch. Good quickness for his size, allows him to separate and make defenders miss in space. Did a much better job of adjusting to off-target throws this season. Little experience as an in-line blocker and it shows with some ugly reps on tape. Can be used as a mismatch weapon all over the offense, either outside, in the slot, or in an H-back role. Ranked 5th among FBS tight ends with 2.63 yards per route. Led all FBS tight ends with 10 deep receptions and 318 deep receiving yards. Ran 81.4 percent of his routes from the slot, 3rd-highest among tight ends.
bottom_line: Andrews was essentially a slot receiver at Oklahoma and he can fill multiple roles at the next level due to his athleticism and ball skills. Like most receiving tight ends in the class, he has work to do in the run game, but he’s capable of lining up in the slot, out wide, or in an H-back role and creating mismatches for opposing defenses.
