Usage will be key, as Andrews works to improve as an in-line blocker, but he has the receiving skills to make an immediate impact.

name: Troy Fumagalli
overview: Solid route runner, can make plays at the intermediate level. Good catch radius. Doesn’t have great athleticism but knows how to use his body and work the middle of the field. Plays right on the border of leveraging defenders and pushing off. Tied for 4th among draft-eligible tight ends with 1.87 yards per route in Caught 45.5 percent of contested targets. Dropped 12 of 147 catchable targets in his career. Provides little after the catch with only four career missed tackles on 135 catches and 3.8 YAC/reception. Continues to improves as a run blocker and can handle first contact. Gives his running back a chance.
bottom_line: Fumagalli knows how the work the middle of the field, using his body and catch radius to move the chains. He’s not a dynamic athlete, and it shows in his subpar after-the-catch stats, but he can be a useful option in the pass game at the short and intermediate level. He’s improved every year as a run blocker and he’s capable of at least holding up against stronger defensive players while also showing the ability to lock onto moving targets.

name: Mike Gesicki
overview: Hauled in four touchdowns out of the slot, third-most among FBS tight ends. Uses his long frame to attack the ball. Good body control to adjust to off- target throws. Caught 75 percent of contested targets (9-for-12), best in the nation among tight ends. Long strides allow him to glide down the field. Inconsistent getting in and out of horizontal routes, but will flash some wiggle at the top of routes. Ranked 31st in the nation with 1.51 yards per route in 2017. Dropped 14 of 146 catchable targets in his career. Had one of the best weeks of practice among tight ends at the Senior Bowl.
bottom_line: Gesicki’s length stands out as he can get up the seam and he uses his frame to make off-target and contested catches. He can be a weapon in the middle of the field, but like many of the tight ends in this class, he’ll have to be used in the right role in the run game. He struggles as an in-line blocker, but was capable enough when asked to block on the move. Gesicki is a mid-tier tight end in this class and he can work well with an aggressive quarterback willing to give him opportunities to win in tight windows.

name: Dallas Goedert
overview: Forced 12 missed tackles after the catch, tied for the first in the nation. Averaged 8.2 yards after the catch per reception. Mismatch weapon in the passing game and South Dakota State got him the ball in a variety of ways. Has the speed to be a vertical threat and the quickness to get off press and win on short routes. Body control allows him to make spectacular catches. Dropped five passes on 76 catchable targets last season. Had 206 run-blocking snaps from a traditional tight end position last season. Not powerful at the point of attack in the run game. Gets to the second level and can locate targets both from tight end or slot alignment.
bottom_line: Goedert should challenge to be the top tight end off the board as he has a fantastic combination of size and athleticism. He moves like a wide receiver despite weighing 260 pounds and he’ll be able to create mismatches at the next level from all over the formation. Goedert looked like a serviceable run-block- er at the FCS level, though he rarely had an opportunity to take on NFL-caliber defensive ends. He’ll make his mark as in the pass game in the NFL, and his size and body control should make him a premier red-zone weapon.

name: Hayden Hurst
overview: Did not drop a pass on 43 catchable passes last season. Only dropped three of 103 catchable targets in his career. Good catch radius and body control. Went 7-for-11 on contested targets (63.6 percent). Has the speed to stretch the seam and the quicks to make defenders miss after the catch. Forced 14 missed tackles on 100 receptions in his career. Averaged 7.0 YAC/reception in his three years. Shows toughness running after the catch. Not afraid of contact. Run blocking is still a work in progress. Misses his target far too often when on the move in the run game. Can fly to the second level in the run game and has a few highlight-reel blocks to his name.
bottom_line: Putting his age aside, Hurst’s athleticism stood out on tape, as he has the speed to work the middle of the field and the quickness and toughness to make plays in the short game. He has potential to create mismatches in the slot or out wide, and he has plenty of experience in a ‘move’ tight end role in South Carolina’s offense. He still has plenty of work to do in the run game, but he’s serviceable in more of an H-back role. Hurst is right up there with the top pass-catchers in this draft.

name: Cam Serigne
overview: Exaggerated route runner. Really tries to sell his breaks. Shows good agility on horizontal routes. Can separate at the break point. Lacks power at the point of attack in the run game. Shows the quickness to reach block and find targets when on the move as a run blocker. Has more in-line experience than most college tight ends. Ran only 35.1 percent of his routes from the slot in 2017. Caught 76.9 percent of his slot targets, 4th-best in the FBS last season. Caught 8-of-13 contested targets (61.5 percent) Forced only 12 missed tackles on 174 career receptions. Dropped 14 passes on 188 catchable targets in his career.
bottom_line: Serigne had a productive four-year career at Wake Forest and he has the route-running ability to be an effective pass-catcher at the next level. He shows some quicks on horizontal routes and he can do damage from multiple po- sitions. He has plenty of experience in-line blocking, but still lacks power in the run game, but he may have the ability to make the necessary blocks on the edge in a zone scheme.

name: Dejon Allen
overview: Undersized college tackle who will likely have to move inside at the next level. False steps in pass protection often. Will need to be completely revamped. Relies on his athleticism at the moment. Slow out of his stance consistently. Will get stood up consistently by NFL edge defenders if he doesn’t fix – especially inside. Thick build through his lower half. Has the frame that could add weight and strength fairly easily. Great lower body drive in the run game. Feet never stop moving. Looks like an athlete out in space. Can locate linebackers at the second level well.
bottom_line: Allen is very much a late-round project at this point. Technically he is nowhere near ready to play in the league, but his athleticism and production are in- triguing. He’s so far away at the moment that his best bet may be to develop on a practice squad.

name: Orlando Brown
overview: As large a human being as you’ll see on a football field. Brown engulfs smaller edge defenders. Impressive length that he knows how to use to his advantage. Makes defenders run a long loop to the quarterback. Strength that you can’t teach. Almost never ceded ground to a bull rush and wasn’t getting taken into the backfield on runs. Slow footed. Simply can’t mirror at a high-level because of his weight. Looks like he’s running in mud on pulls. Inconsistent with technique from snap to snap. Possibly scheme limited with his movement ability. Not a guy you want playing in space too often.
bottom_line: Brown’s highest levels makes you think he’s a future All-Pro, but his lowest ones give you pause about him matching up with NFL-caliber athletes. In the right scheme though, it will be easy to fall in love with Brown and his sheer physical prowess. You hope he can lean out in an NFL training facility and get some quickness back in his game.

name: Zachary Crabtree
overview: Right tackle with the size to stay there at the NFL level. Four-year starter at right tackle who was one of the best pass protectors in country as junior and senior. Allowed 16 pressures in 2017. Plodder. Mirror ability is subpar and got out-quicked by even average college athletes on the edge. Proficient gaining depth and playing angles in pass protection. Smooth in and out of stance. Not an overly powerful tackle. Showed in run game, where he never graded too far above average. Locating linebackers in space looked like a chore. Athleticism leaves a lot to be desired. Rarely latches into defender’s shoulder pads and locks out. More often than not just leans on guys in run game.
bottom_line: Crabtree may very well be capped out as far as his capabilities go. He lacks the requisite quickness to match NFL caliber athletes on the edge. Some of that could be alleviated by a move to guard, but his overall poor leverage makes that unlikely to be a much better fit.

name: Tyrell Crosby
overview: Multiple seasons of elite grades at both right and left tackle. Thick, strong tackle who owns a power advantage against almost every defensive lineman he faced. Run blocks with a mean streak. When his hand placement is on point he buries defensive linemen. Feet are slow and mirroring ability suffers as a result. Made a living off his strength and ability to snatch defenders in pass pro. Rarely took true pass sets at Oregon. Keeps hands wide and gets grabby when he did. At his best when he can play straight ahead. Could be scheme limited in the NFL. Not great in space.
bottom_line: Crosby isn’t going to win any beauty contests with his play style, but he got the job done at a high level at Oregon. It’s encouraging that he showed well in pass protection 1-on-1s at the Senior Bowl, with a 67 percent win rate, considering his pass sets at Oregon were underdeveloped. His quickness could even see teams value him as a guard at the next level.

name: Jeromy Irwin
overview: Three-year starter at left tackle (missed most of 2015 due to injury) who improved every single year at Colorado. One of the best pass protectors in the nation and only allowed six sacks his entire college career. Top-heavy big man who struggles to play with leverage. Often stands straight up on first contact with defender. Balance is a big issue and unlikely one that has a quick fix. Wins more with technique in pass-pro than athleticism. First punch is solid, but feet are too slow to recover if it doesn’t land. Strong upper body that can torque defenders in the run game and stop them in their tracks in pass pro.
bottom_line: Irwin’s college production this past season was fantastic, but there are a lot of concerns about it translating to the NFL. With his lack of athleticism, he’s a strong candidate to kick inside to guard at the next level. The quicker he can get into defenders the better, it allows his natural strength can take over.

name: Jamarco Jones
overview: Well built, strong tackle with two-years of starting experience coming off a breakout season in 2017. Only allowed 11 total pressures this past season. Adept independent hand usage in pass protection. Long arms that he knows how to use. Great depth out of his kick slide for a big man. Didn’t take a ton of true pass sets, but already looks well developed in that regard. Doesn’t play with consistent leverage. Won’t always sink hips on contact in run game instead opting to lurch into blocks. Gets off-balance easily and doesn’t always play under control.
bottom_line: Jones has all the tools to play tackle at the next level, but he’s not a finished product yet. His pass sets are a thing of beauty and he should only improve with more experience in an NFL passing game. He rarely flashed dominant potential, but you don’t need to be a dominant run blocker to be a high-level tackle in today’s NFL.

name: Kc Mcdermott
overview: Three-year starter who graded out better every successive season of his college career. Waist bender. Gets himself in a lot of bad situations because of that and is easily knocked off balance. Strong hands that won’t let go once he’s locked on. Easily his biggest strength. Plays with hands low and wide. Very inconsistent with his punch and technique. Needs to add a good deal of strength to play in the NFL and it’s unclear if he’ll ever get there. Feet can be a nightmare in times in pass pro. All over the place.
bottom_line: McDermott’s development has been encouraging, but he’s still some ways away from being an NFL tackle. He has the size of one, but not the strength or athlet- icism. He’ll have an uphill climb to ever start in the league and may ultimately be a guard.

name: Mike Mcglinchey
overview: Looks the part in every regard. Size, length, strength, and athleticism are all top notch. Has graded extremely well every single year of his career. Even after making the switch from right to left tackle. Had some dominant outings. Two of his four highest graded games this season came against extremely talented fronts of USC and NC State. Formed the best double team combo in the country with left guard Quenton Nelson. Moved DTs multiple yards off ball almost every time. Inconsistent with his punch in pass protection. Had his hands swatted away far too easily at times. Carries hands low in pass sets and leaves his chest open. Will be susceptible to bull rush in NFL.
bottom_line: McGlinchey is as clean as any tackle prospect in this class, but there are a handful of things on his tape that still are concerning. He has a lot more de- cisive losses than you’d like from a tackle you’re taking at the top of the draft and his traits aren’t necessarily ‘elite.’ He still figures to be a high pick who can start at either tackle position from day one.

name: Kolton Miller
overview: Size, length, and build of an NFL tackle. Good enough athlete to get out and move in the run game. Not scheme limited. Plays high and isn’t strong enough to make up for it. Can get rocked into the backfield. Very wide feet in pass protection. Feet can stop on contact and he struggles to recover. Solid hand usage in the running game. Consistent with his placement. Good awareness of stunts and blitzes in pass protection.
bottom_line: Miller looks the part of an NFL tackle, but his strength and athleticism don’t get evaluators particularly excited. He took a big step forward this past season and was one of the most effective pass protectors in college football. He’ll need to add a good deal of strength to be a plus pass protector at the NFL level.

name: Chukwuma Okorafor
overview: Looks the part from a size and length perspective. Moves like an athlete when he’s out in space. Slow out of stance and chasing from backside on zone plays. Lackadaisical punch in pass protection. Long arms, but doesn’t yet know how to use them to his advantage. Lacks a mean streak. Possesses rare physical traits, but almost never saw him impose his will on defenders. Feet get all over the place in pass protection. Gets himself in bad situations too often. Strong upper body that can toss and ragdoll defensive linemen. Three-year starter with experience at both tackle spots.
bottom_line: Okorafor is nothing more than a project at this point. He’s not ready to step on an NFL field day one, but could be a few years down the line if he puts it all to- gether. Only earned an average 76.4 grade this past season against MAC com- petition. His game will need to be built from the ground up at the next level.

name: Brian O’neill
overview: Fantastic athlete for the position. Moves about as well as any tackle in this class. Mirrors extremely well. Can get out of his stance quickly and maintain favorable relationship with edge rushers. Punch in pass pro does him no favors. Weak and easily slapped away by defenders. Was awful in Senior Bowl 1-on-1s. Only won 27 percent of his reps throughout the week. Play strength is nothing special. Not a people mover. Likely zone scheme limited. Oversets at times and is susceptible to inside counters.
bottom_line: After a dominant 2016 season where he allowed all of four pressures all year, O’Neill took a step back in 2017. His Senior Bowl performance is incredibly worrisome, as he was dominated by the better competition. He’ll need to add strength to have a chance of starting early in the league.

name: Martinas Rankin
overview: Initial punch is completely deadening when it lands. Long arms with the strength to stop defenders in their tracks. Slow feet that struggle mirroring any sort of quickness. Allowed 18 pressures in 247 pass-blocking snaps. Allowed two sacks, a hit, and three hurries in a dreadful performance against Mississippi this season. Struggles sustaining blocks. Even when he gets initial engage, he loses control of far too many blocks. Attacks blocks high in the run game and doesn’t play with leverage as well as you’d like. Had some dominant blocks leading out in front of screens.
bottom_line: Rankin improved from 2016 to 2017, but still graded out as a below-average college tackle this past season. He’s likely not athletic enough to hold up on the outside in the NFL and is ultimately better suited for guard or center. Even there he’s a project though, as his hands aren’t good enough to draft highly there.

name: Will Richardson
overview: Long, lean tackle with requisite build to hold up on the edge in the NFL. Explosive at the point of contact. Regularly rocks back edge players and widens point of attack. Tight splits of the offensive linemen at N.C. State often masked some of his agility deficiencies. Waist bending is a serious concern with him. Often out over his toes and easily gets off-balance. Gets good depth and mirrors well in his pass sets. Feet never stop moving. Patient in pass protection. Doesn’t go searching for the first punch and lets the defender come to him.
bottom_line: Richardson has been suspended multiple times throughout his college career and his off-field will need thorough vetting. He offers much more than most day two and day three tackles, though. He could stand to add some strength to his frame but has all the tools to be a starting tackle in time.

name: Connor Williams
overview: Elite athlete for tackle position. Can execute any block asked of him. Has been a dominant college tackle from the first day he stepped on the field. Allowed all of four hurries his sophomore season in 2016. Took a bit of a step back in 2017 and played only 332 snaps through injuries. Very few true pass sets in Texas’ offense. Still a work in progress in that regard. Well-proportioned for his size. Carries 300-plus pounds with ease. Strong frame throughout. Hand placement in the run game is fantastic. Gets hands inside play after play. Doesn’t get enough depth consistently in his pass sets.
bottom_line: Williams has multiple seasons of production as one of the top tackles in college football. If he would have been able to come out in the draft a season ago, he’d likely go higher than he will now after disappointing this past season. Still, Williams has high-level traits and grading that make him a day one pros- pect.

name: Colby Gossett
overview: Four strong years of grading, though 2017 represented the lowest grade of his four-year career. Can turn defenders when on the move on front side of zone runs. Loses on first contact too often in the run game. Experience in a zone-heavy scheme and can make all of the necessary blocks in an outside-zone heavy system. Late to recognize blitzing linebackers. Looks for work when uncovered in pass protection. Has solid tape at right tackle, playing 172 snaps there in 2016 and 433 snaps in 2015. Experienced. Has played 3,162 career snaps. Allowed only 36 pressures on 1,313 career snaps in pass protection.
bottom_line: Gossett had an excellent career at Appalachian State, capping it off with a solid week at the Senior Bowl. His experience in a zone-blocking scheme should translate well at the next level, and his size, length and experience at right tackle give him some versatility. Gossett makes difficult run blocks look easy, but he must improve his consistency on the “easy” stuff in order to maximize his value. He’s worth a look in the middle of the draft.

name: Will Hernandez
overview: Truly dominated the competition at UTEP. His 95.2 overall grade in 2016 is the highest single season grade we’ve ever given to a guard. Has the anchor of an aircraft carrier. Good luck bull rushing him. Allowed all of four pressures in the past two seasons combined. Not infallible in pass protection though. Struggled with speed and when defensive tackles got into his shoulder pads at the Senior Bowl. Thickly built frame from top to bottom. Fire hydrant who out-muscled every single player he went against. Iffy locating in space. When he gets a clear line of sight and can deliver a blow, it’s scary. Slow footed. Can stop his feet in pass protection and fails to recover when taken of balance.
bottom_line: Hernandez is such a fun prospect to evaluate because his strengths and weak- nesses are so well defined. He’s a certified people moverr who will be a weapon on double teams from day one. Hernandez isn’t the most fleet of foot, however, and would be best suited in a gap scheme that asks him to fire off the ball.

name: Cole Madison
overview: One of the best track records in pass protection of any tackle in the class grade-wise. The pass sets at Washington State aren’t the same as he’ll be taking in the NFL. Will have to be completely reworked. Good feet and mirror. Rarely got himself into bad situations. Athleticism overall is poor. Showed up a lot in the screen game where he struggled to locate. Plays high far too often and can get bowled over because of it. Very susceptible to the bull rush. Projection in the run game. Barely utilized at Washington State and concepts/technique weren’t what he’ll be running in NFL.
bottom_line: Madison has already shown to be proficient in pass protection throughout his career, but there’s a lot of question marks about whether it will translate to the NFL level. His strength and overall athleticism are below-average for NFL tackles and he projects better as a guard.

name: Quenton Nelson
overview: Far and away the highest graded guard in college football this past season with a 95.1 overall grade. Graded above 90.0 in 2016 as well. Plays to the whistle snap after snap. Never met a block he didn’t want to finish with the defender on the ground. Flashes power at the line of scrimmage as well as on pull blocks. Can generate movement off the line of scrimmage on nearly any type of block. Freakish blend of athleticism and flexibility. Wins the leverage battle regularly. Natural aggression can be detriment at times when he gets overextended trying to deliver a blow. Pass sets look like instant replays. Technique is consistent snap after snap with a deadening, quick punch.
bottom_line: The most dominant offensive line process in our four years of PFF College. Could legitimately play tackle at the next level, as the only reason he started at guard in the first place was because Notre Dame had future first rounders at both tackle positions (Ronnie Stanley and Mike McGlinchey).

name: Braden Smith
overview: Plays angry. Feet never stop churning and plays consistently to the whistle. Has a constant forward lean. Gets off-balance on contact too often because of it. Has a hitch in his giddy-up when coming out of his stance on pulls. Looks unnatural in space. Choppy with his feet and slower to locate than you’d like. Strong as an ox. Regularly moves the line of scrimmage even on 1-on-1 blocks. Late reacting in pass pro on blitzes and stunts.
bottom_line: Smith is a home run hitter type of guard who will alternate dominant reps with whiffs. You can’t teach his strength though, and he’s going to be drafted highly because of it. He’s far from a perfect prospect, but he’s an easy projection with how advanced he is as a run blocker already.

name: Wyatt Teller
overview: Bulldozer in the run game. Had some of the most impressive blocks in the country this year. Destroyed some defenders. A little tight in the hips. Really shows up when asked to change directions. Ducks his head into blocks far more than you’d like. Can be impatient in pass pro. When he gets his hands inside a defender’s shoulder pads it’s game over. He’s not letting go. As powerful a guard as you’ll see in a compact frame. Was running with defensive tackles at times. Can get a narrow base in pass protection that causes balance issues.
bottom_line: Teller has been one of the highest graded guards in the country for four straight seasons now, but it’s concerning that he took a slight step backwards as a senior instead of taking his game to the elite-level. The level of play he’s sustained throughout his career though is hard to ignore, and he’s got all the tools to succeed in the NFL.

name: Isaiah Wynn
overview: Undersized tackle who likely profiles to the interior in the NFL. Still got the job done in pass protection despite his height. Only allowed five pressures all season long and 26 in 2,609 snaps for his career. Dominated the week at the Senior Bowl. Was highest graded player in 1-on-1s and he only lost two reps. Extremely consistent. Plays under control snap after snap. Very polished already. Could step in and start from day one. Plays with solid natural leverage. May not be the strongest, but still generates movement.
bottom_line: Wynn is one of the most talented offensive line prospects in this draft. He’ll have to make the transition from tackle to guard or center, but the track record of players successfully making that switch is so vast that it’s not even a point of concern. He’s an incredibly clean prospect otherwise and should be taken highly as a result.

name: Brian Allen
overview: Great natural leverage. Comes out of stance low and under control. Below average athlete. Really shows when asked to get out and pull the edge and locate. Noticeable hitch in his pull. Experience at both guard (2016) and center (2017), but size profiles best to center in the NFL. Short-arms and struggles to maintain engage with longer defensive tackles. Issue in both run and pass game. Rarely takes opposition off the line of scrimmage. Wins mostly via control rather than brute force. Never looked overmatched by an opponent at the college level. No poorly graded games over last two seasons.
bottom_line: Allen has been one of the best offensive linemen in college football each of the past two seasons, but he doesn’t check a ton of NFL boxes physically. Allen is an undersized center who doesn’t quite have the athleticism to make up for the lack of strength. As technically sound as he is, Allen is still a solid option later in the draft.

name: Bradley Bozeman
overview: Lynchpin to one of the best offensive lines in football over the past couple of seasons. Technician with his hand placement. Great independent hand usage in run and pass game. Only allowed 10 total pressures in his college career (2,220 total snaps). Core strength isn’t great. Can get flat-backed fairly easily by defensive tackles 1-on-1. Plodder. Likely scheme limited at the next level with his lack of athleticism. Can get knocked off balance far too easily. Seemed to be always on the verge of falling on his face.
bottom_line: Bozeman is going to have an uphill climb to ever become an NFL starter with his athleticism. He got the job done for multiple seasons in the SEC though and it didn’t seem to a huge hindrance there. Bozeman has the size to play either guard or center and that versatility will be looked favorably upon in the

name: Will Clapp
overview: Experience in a pro-style scheme at LSU playing both guard and center. Three straight seasons of quality grades playing against top quality competition. Very consistent with his technique already. Almost robotic in the way he goes about his business. Plays very much under control. Rarely overextends himself or ends up on the ground. Lacking high-level physical traits. The dominant blocks are few and far between. Well-timed punch in pass protection. Hardly any whiffs on tape. Only eight pressures allowed this past season.
bottom_line: Clapp was and extremely solid if unspectacular player for LSU over the past three seasons. He has the ability to play both guard and center while maintain- ing a high level of play. The only thing he’s lacking is the ‘wow’ factor at this point because he checks a ton of other boxes to be a starting interior offensive lineman in the NFL.

name: Mason Cole
overview: Four-year starter who bounced back and forth between left tackle and center throughout his career. Coming off the best season of his career in 2017, where he allowed a total of 17 pressures at left tackle. Got torn apart by Nick Bosa and Ohio State this past season. Exposed weak punch in pass protection. Hails from pro-style running game at Michigan that asked him to execute numerous different blocks. Ducks into blocks with wide hands. Struggles to maintain a clean engage as a result. Nothing special strength wise. Not a line of scrimmage mover by any means.
bottom_line: Likely best suited to be a center in the NFL, Cole could play guard and maybe even tackle in a pinch as well. That versatility will be coveted, but not enough to warrant a high draft pick. He may not be a super exciting prospect, but he’s fairly clean and has a huge body of work to evaluate off of.

name: Austin Corbett
overview: Four-year starter at left tackle for Nevada. Only allowed 23 total pressures on his last two seasons. Keeps hands tight in both the run game and in pass protection – regularly hitting his strike zone. Can get antsy trying to deliver a deadening punch in pass pro. That aggressiveness can be used against him at times. Plays to the whistle. Often times saw him carrying linebackers offscreen that didn’t want any part of him. Gets good depth out of his pass sets and cuts down angles quickly on edge rushers. Active with his hands. Has the size and athleticism to play multiple positions along the offensive line.
bottom_line: Corbett is a touch undersized for an NFL tackle, but has all the traits neces- sary to hold up there. He’s far more technically sound than most small school offensive linemen and even with the huge jump in competition he could start sooner rather than later.

name: James Daniels
overview: Very productive center. Hails from an Iowa offense whose concepts closely mirror that of NFL offenses. Consistently under control. Patient almost to a fault at times. Great feel for zone blocking scheme. Not much of a people mover. Taken into the backfield more than you’d like to see from a college center. Play strength overall can be issue, as he struggled with bull rush at times. Locating linebackers was an adventure for him at times. Once he gets moving in space, he really struggled to change directions. Biggest pass pro issue was recovering to the looper on stunts. Feet and reaction time both slow. Allowed 10 pressures this past season.
bottom_line: Iowa head coach Kirk Ferentz called Daniels the most NFL ready center he’s ever coached. That’s high praise with the linemen Iowa has put out and the grades back it up. He’s been one of college football’s best centers each of the past two seasons. Daniels is far from a perfect prospect, but he’s close enough to step in and contribute on an NFL field next season.

name: Billy Price
overview: Has played all three interior positions at some point in his career at Ohio State. LG as freshman/sophomore. RG as junior. C as senior. Nastiness that offensive line coaches love. Is out for blood on every snap. Very active hands. Even when he doesn’t get initial placement perfect, he’s quick to reset and regain control. Overextends in pass protection for his punch. Lots of quick losses in pass protection as a result. Speed gives him problems. Aggressiveness gets him in trouble in run game as well. Always looking for the kill shot. Power is superb for the position. Can line up a target and take them yards downfield.
bottom_line: Price is the rare four-year starter at a major college program and that itself is enough to get evaluators attention. He’s far from a perfect prospect, though, as he’s had inconsistencies on tape still this past season that you’d have hoped would be cleaned up by now. He alternates ugly blocks with dominant ones that NFL coaches will think they can harness every snap.

name: Scott Quessenberry
overview: Fantastic athlete for the position. Quick off the snap and reaches shades with ease. Play strength is lacking. Struggled to take even college defensive tackles off the line of scrimmage. Loses control of blocks at the line of scrimmage too easily. Hands struggle to latch on consistently. Got dominated in the week of practices leading up to the Senior Bowl. Lowest graded offensive lineman in the 1-on-1s. Athleticism doesn’t translate to quick feet in pass protection. Had issues recovering and passing off stunts. Three-year starter with experience at guard as well as center.
bottom_line: Quessenberry is a perfect fit for teams that like to get their centers out on the move. Whether that be a team that is outside zone heavy or pulls their center to the edge – the UCLA product can do either. He also has some positional flex- ibility and could hold up at guard. His strength limitations are obvious though and it’s concerning how overpowered he was in the Senior Bowl 1-on-1s.

name: Frank Ragnow
overview: Consistently dominant on-field performance when healthy over the last two seasons. PFF’s highest graded center in 2016 & 2017. Some of the best hands of any offensive linemen in this class. Placement and strength are both consistently elite. Not going to be mistaken for Jason Kelce anytime soon, but is more than a capable athlete to play in any offensive scheme. Great feel for timing on combo blocks. Sprung a ton of big runs by climbing to pick off a linebacker at exact right time. Allowed all of 15 total pressures over the past two seasons. Feet can be slow to recover and could struggle with quicker linebackers and nose tackles at next level. Thing of beauty watching him fire off the ball 1-on-1 into a nose tackle. Play strength is top notch.
bottom_line: Ragnow checks almost all the boxes one could want from a center other than his health (senior year ended with high-ankle injury). He’s a three-year starter with dominant tape that has experience at both guard (2015) and center (2016 and 2017). The Arkansas center has also done it against top competition in the SEC and never once looked overmatched.

name: Edge Olasunkanmi Adeniyi
overview: Finished with 14 sacks, 38 hits, and 51 hurries on 698 career rushes. Ranked 2nd among the nation’s edge defenders with 20 hits in 2017. Much smaller than most NFL edge defenders. May struggle to use entire array of pass-rush moves due to lack of length. Tenacious. Doesn’t have as many quick wins as other top edge defenders but keeps after the quarterback as a rusher. Can win to the outside, but still not enough clean wins in which he clears the offensive tackle on the way to the quarterback. Can get engulfed in the run game if he doesn’t win upon first contact. Had the 52nd-highest percentage of negatively graded plays against the run in 2017. Uses good low pad level to beat blockers in the run game. Had the 7th- highest percentage of positively graded plays against the run in 2017.
bottom_line: The NFL may be scared of Adeniyi’s lack of size and length, but his production warrants a shot at the next level. His lack of size works for him at times, as he can get under blockers both as a pass-rusher and in the run game, though he’ll also get engulfed and taken out of plays as well. Adeniyi may get an initial look as a situational pass-rusher and he has a chance to carry his production from college to the NFL.

name: Edge Lorenzo Carter
overview: Flashed dominant potential at times. Took over the Notre Dame game early in season with eight pressures. Dropped into coverage frequently in Georgia’s scheme. Only rushed the passer on 192 snaps this past season. Elite length. Doesn’t always use it well, but when he does he can keep himself clean. Average athlete. Get off doesn’t do him any favors and had trouble finishing on ball carriers. Doesn’t especially like playing through contact. Finesse type player. Slightly built and play strength is lacking. Has the type of frame that can put on more weight and he needs to.
bottom_line: Carter looked like a first-rounder at times this past season, but a UDFA at oth- ers. His lack of consistency will certainly push him down draft boards, but it’s easy to fall in love with some of his plays. Ultimately though, Carter’s athleti- cism and overall production leave a lot to be desired. If he can put some added muscle on his frame, he can be a solid edge setter at the next level.

name: Edge Bradley Chubb
overview: Has rare explosiveness for a 270-plus pound human being. Not many men his size can legitimately press the upfield shoulder of tackles like he can. A handful in the run game. Good luck getting movement on him if he doesn’t want to be moved. Struggled against best offensive line he faced in Notre Dame. Only registered three pressures all game. Bull rush could be his go-to, but was rarely employed while at N.C. State. Had a few long arm rushes that were nearly unstoppable. Advanced hand usage as a pass-rusher already. Can win in a variety of different ways Very stiff turning the corner. Had more than a few rushes where he won the edge then either fell or got washed out of play from slight push.
bottom_line: Chubb is such an easy projection because his game is already so well devel- oped. He’s a big, powerful base end that knows how to use his hands and could kick inside while still being solid against both run and pass. He’s improved every season of his career and never had games where he completely disap- peared. Ultimately though, he may be capped as a pass-rusher by his flexibility and doesn’t profile as a high sack total type of edge rusher.

name: Edge Marcus Davenport
overview: Physically imposing edge defender. The kind of height (6-foot-7) and length (34” arms) that teams crave setting the edge. Raw as can be. Needs to be taught pass-rushing technique from the ground up. Bull rush is go to move and even that could use some refining. Overpowered tackles in Conference USA. Lack of pass-rush repertoire apparent at Senior Bowl, where he won only 38 percent of reps in 1-on-1s. Pop on first contact in run game and as pass-rusher is special. Not many edge defenders even in NFL have his tools. Lined up almost exclusively against right tackles. Only took 127 snaps from right side all last season.
bottom_line: Davenport is currently a collection of parts that have yet to be assembled into a working vehicle. The good news is that he could very well be a Ferrari if they’re ever put together, but there’s no way of knowing when and if that will happen. His upward grade progression in college is encouraging, as was his playmak- ing ability with 36 total stops this past season, but he’s still pure projection at this point.

name: Edge Duke Ejiofor
overview: Looks the part from a size/athleticism perspective. Very active hands. Never done as a pass-rusher and can win late. Employed the rare outside spin move more than a few times and made it work. Kicked inside on third downs and can be used as a chess piece at the NFL level. Calculated pass-rusher. Not simply a one-move type of guy. Bases his moves on how the tackle plays him. Linear upward progression throughout his college career. Not overly explosive. No real high-level traits.
bottom_line: Ejiofor was the definition of solid at Wake Forest this past season. He had at least three pressures all but one full game he played this year. There’s not much about him that really pops off the tape, but he consistently gets the job done nonetheless. His ability to rush the passer from the interior is a legiti- mate weapon that can be taken advantage of in the NFL.

name: Edge Kylie Fitts
overview: Rarely won to the inside or with a bullrush. Must expand his pass-rush repertoire. Battled injuries throughout his career. Played 658 snaps in 2015 and only 600 snaps in 2016 and 2017 combined. Has the agility to turn the corner on the edge. Led the nation with nine batted passes in 2015. Plays with good leverage in the run game. Regularly dominated 1-on-1 matchups with tight ends. Disrupting and disengaging in order to make plays. Feels the downblock and takes out pullers when playing power/counter. Can get engulfed or washed down the line of scrimmage by better offensive tackles in the run game.
bottom_line: Fitts is a classic case of having all of the necessary tools but not being able to put it all together on the field. His career looked promising after an excellent 2015 season, but injuries and inconsistency derailed what could have been. Fitts is worth a shot to see if he can regain his previous trajectory that had him looking like one of the nation’s top pass-rushers in 2015.

name: Edge Jeff Holland
overview: Majority of wins came to the outside of offensive tackles. Must expand his entire repertoire of pass-rush moves. Lacks the desired size for NFL edge rushers. Despite lack of size, has good length and showed effective stab moves to get under offensive tackles. Effective on stunts, either when coming unblocked or when navigating through blocks. Productive pass-rusher but did not have a high percentage of dominant 1-on-1 wins against good offensive tackles. Only one year of strong production. 65 of his 95 career pressures came in Will disrupt blockers in the running game but struggles to finish. Had a run-stop percentage of only 5.9 percent last season.
bottom_line: Holland is one of a few undersized yet productive rushers in this class. While he may not fit the traditional mold on the outside, and he lacks desired three- down ability, there are things to like about his game and he may be best used as a movable chess piece in the pass-rush game. His effectiveness rushing off the edge should lend to production as a blitzer if used to move around for isolated matchups against running backs at the next level.

name: Edge Sam Hubbard
overview: Ideal build for the position at 6-6, 265 pounds. Ability to play a number of different alignments at that size. Nothing special athletically. Noticeably a step slower out of stance than line mates at Ohio State. Never done as a pass-rusher. Won’t get himself in bad positions and is just as likely to win with his second/third move as his first. Two-hand swipe is his go to move and will consistently fight tackles up high. Played only 528 snaps in 14 games and still had some slow reps. Never dominated a game from start to finish. Not overly powerful. Has to win with technique rather than physically imposing his will on offensive tackles. Even when he wins, can struggle to close on quarterback and was often times taken off balance by slight nudges
bottom_line: Hubbard’s evaluation is an exercise in what one values most from edge rush- ers, because his strengths and weaknesses are so defined. He’s NFL ready from a technical standpoint, but nearly every elite edge rusher in the league is a far better athlete. He may not excite, but he could step on an NFL field today and be productive.

name: Edge Arden Key
overview: Fits the long and lean mold of LSU edge defenders standing 6-6, 255 pounds with long arms. Took a leave of absence from LSU for personal reasons last spring and came back in the fall a tad heavier and slower after shoulder surgery. Freakish body control for his size. Could pass as a wide receiver his sophomore year the way he could dip and change direction. Rip is his go to move, but bull-rush is still a work in progress. Has all the tools to make it work in time though. Uninterested at times versus run. Struggles to hold the point against powerful tackles and can get out-leveraged. High end is arguably the most impressive in the class. Graded well against last year’s first round tackle Ryan Ramczyk.
bottom_line: Key’s off the field evaluation may be as important as his on-field at this point. His grade dropped from 87.8 as a sophomore to 81.1 as a junior, which is just an added red flag. He’s arguably the most physically gifted pass-rusher in this class and dominated the SEC as a sophomore, but he still has a ways to go tech- nically. The question is will he be focused enough to put it all together?

name: Edge Harold Landry
overview: As twitchy an athlete as you’ll find in this draft class. Would at times beat college tackles with no more than his first step. Bend around the edge is elite. Can dip and play at an angle with the best of them. Something was very off with him senior year. Wasn’t close to same player from junior tape. Missed last four games with ankle injury. Too often a one-move pass-rusher. If he doesn’t win on contact he’s taken out of the play. Sells out too often for sacks. Flashed speed-to-power, but strength is still an issue. Tad undersized and could be seen as a designated pass-rusher. He’s not much of a hands fighter as a pass-rusher, though he knows how to work his hands on his rips and outside moves. Gets himself into trouble telegraphing directions without being able to counter. Could be deadly with his speed and more developed counter.
bottom_line: The difference between Landry’s junior year tape (89.0 overall grade) and senior year (83.9) is terrifying. Teams will have to do their due diligence as to why that’s the case, but it could be as simple as a lingering ankle injury that ended his season. His junior season was the best we’ve seen from anyone in this class as a pass-rusher, and his off-the-charts athleticism suggests he will translate to the next level.

name: Edge Justin Lawler
overview: Finished with 23 sacks, 24 hits, and 100 hurries on 1,019 career rushes. Knows how to win with low pad level and quick hands. Attacks offensive linemen with a variety of pass-rush moves. Wins to the outside and with power. Powerfully works through contact on his way to the quarterback. Capped a strong week of practice at the Shrine Game, capping it with a sack and two run stops in the game. Disruptive player but was often a step slow converting pressures into sacks. Posted at least six pressures in six different games in 2017. Explodes into blockers in the run game. Can dominate both sides of the block, especially against tight ends. Had the 3rd-lowest percentage of negatively graded plays against the run among edge defenders in 2017.
bottom_line: Lawler put together multiple seasons of strong play, culminating in a domi- nant 2017. He wins with low pad level and strong technique, both attributes that often go overlooked when it comes to the draft process. While Lawler may not have the same athleticism as the top edge defenders in the class, he knows how to defeat blocks in both the run game and as a pass-rusher, and that gives him a chance to become a productive NFL player.

name: Edge Tyquan Lewis
overview: A player that has aligned in multiple spots, played inside and outside on the D-line at Ohio State. Box score stats declined in 2017, but grades did not. Still notched 44 total pressures. Incredibly reliable tackler. Missed just nine across four years, with only one miss in 2017. A tweener who looked more effective inside in college but doesn’t have the size for that at the next level. Can struggle to hold up against strength, particularly on down-blocks or double teams where he gets rocked off his spot. Has some explosiveness but lacks consistent agility and speed to attack the edge. Dominated in the Senior Bowl, with six total pressures on 22 pass- rushing snaps.
bottom_line: Lewis has been a productive player for Ohio State and done so in a variety of different D-line techniques along their front. Averaged 47 total pressures and 20 defensive stops over the past two seasons. Needs to prove he can play on the edge at the next level, because he doesn’t have the size or strength to hold up inside. Was very productive in the Senior Bowl, but not so much during the week of practices. Will hit an NFL roster, and then needs to show he can still be productive at the next level.

name: Egde Hercules Mata’afa
overview: Played out of position all season long on the interior of Washington State’s defense. Only took seven snaps outside the tackles all season. Fantastic athlete who often times had to do little more than slant across an offensive lineman’s face at the snap to win. Comfortable fighting through traffic with terrific bend. Go to move as a rip on the interior and was usually all he needed. Doesn’t have a refined pass-rushing skill set. Really only used his hands when he had already beaten a Offensive lineman to get himself clean. Great balance as a pass-rusher or run defender. Had to face the double teams that came on inside and held up well. Didn’t play in space often, but when he did his closing ability was special.
bottom_line: It’s impossible to know what Mata’afa will look like facing offensive tackles snap after snap because he’s never done it. If you’re going to take a chance on a guy who played out of position though, I’d do it with a player like Mata’afa, who still graded extremely well while playing defensive tackle. All the traits are there, but he’ll need good coaching and patience at the next level.

name: Edge Uchenna Nwosu
overview: Agility that is immediately apparent on tape. Can stop on a dime and change directions during his pass-rush. Undersized for the position. Has to be on the edge and may even be limited to designated pass-rusher. Had an incredible 10 batted passes this past season. One-year wonder. Had three sacks and 43 total pressures to his name in three seasons before 10 sacks and 63 pressures this season. Disappeared when he didn’t have a drastic athletic advantage over the opposing tackle. Legitimate coverage ability. Could even be seen as an off-ball linebacker by certain teams.
bottom_line: Nwosu is a perfect fit for teams that utilize a true 3-4 outside linebacker. He’s a capable underneath zone defender whose athleticism can be used as a weapon on blitzes/stunts. As a pure pass-rusher, he’s nothing special, often getting by on little more than his athleticism. It’s encouraging the strides he’s already made from early in his career though.

name: Edge Ogbonnia Okoronkwo
overview: Undersized at 6-1, but with exceptional length (34” arms) that can still get it done on the edge at the NFL level. Showed well at the Senior Bowl, with 50 percent win rate in 1-on-1s (second best of any edge) and was highest graded defender in game. Fantastic natural leverage with his size allows him to play bigger than his weight (242) suggests. Not limited to pass-rusher only. Deadly inside spin move when employed. Has the balance for it to be a consistent weapon that offensive linemen have to worry about. Not the most physical of pass-rushers. Will get sack happy and just try to run around linemen instead of playing through them. Great lateral agility. Can often beat tackles with his quickness alone and can stop on a dime for an inside counter. Not a ‘bend the edge’ type of pass-rusher despite his size. Can be a little stiff when ripping to the edge.
bottom_line: There are too many strikes against Okoronkwo (size/flexibility) to feel com- fortable pounding the table for him at the top of the draft, but he offers a legit pass-rushing skillset that can contribute right away. He was the second-high- est graded Power-5 edge defender this past season (87.5) and was a complete player at Oklahoma. He’ll need to add strength to play full-time at the next level, but he’s not too far off.

name: Edge Joe Ostman
overview: Some of the best hand usage in this entire class. Fights snap after snap with a myriad of moves to keep himself clean. Terrific balance. Plays extremely well through contact to finish. Had 45 total stops this past season. Competition is a major concern. Kansas, Syracuse, and Boston College were his only power five opponents this year. One-year wonder who saw his grade leap from 80.8 to 91.1 this past season. Undersized. Holding up against the run may be an issue at the next level and teams may even see him as an off-ball linebacker. Limited athletically and not particularly flexible. Doesn’t ‘look the part’.
bottom_line: Ostman has maxed out his physical attributes about as well as one can. He’s undersized and even against MAC competition he doesn’t pop off the tape ath- letically, but he was a handful for every tackle he faced. If he can get his weight up while maintaining his play speed, he’ll have a chance in the league.

name: Edge Ja’von Rolland-Jones
overview: Slightly built, speed rusher who was simply too athletic for many of the tackles he faced in the Sun Belt. Never had to develop his hand usage to win against lesser competition. A lot of pass-rushes with no plan of attack. The rare small school prospect with NFL caliber athleticism and flexibility. Pops off the tape right away. Size is a big issue. Will need to gain a considerable amount of weight to play in the NFL. Bull rush was nearly non-existent. Much more of a finesse than power player. Likely limited to a designated pass-rusher.
bottom_line: Rolland-Jones is the kind of player whose athletic testing numbers will play a big role in his evaluation. He needs to add a good deal of weight from his play- ing days at Arkansas State and it’s unclear if he can still be the same high-level athlete with added strength. He’s not particularly refined at this point, but still was incredibly productive at the college level.

name: Edge Kentavius Street
overview: Incredibly powerful and low to the ground, able to leverage his way through players while turning the corner as a pass-rusher. Shows good bend around the edge when he commits to dipping around a tackle, but too often relies solely on power. Has consistently been a better run defender than pass-rusher, with 20 defensive stops and only four missed tackles in 2017. Too keen to engage and hand fight tackles rather than beating them on contact with a pass-rush move. Dominated at the Shrine game with two sacks and eight total pressures on just 31 pass-rushing snaps. Needs to either develop his pass-rush moves on the edge, or kick inside to exploit his power and leverage. Street sustained a torn ACL in a private workout with the New York Giants on April 4th, likely costing him his entire rookie season.
bottom_line: An intriguing player with monstrous power, Street has been a powerful run de- fender in his college career but only really generated pressure as an edge rush- er with power. He does show the ability to dip and bend, but seeks to engage rather than defeat blocks, which leads to him being eliminated by top tackles. He did dominate the East-West Shrine game, and isn’t far off the necessary size to kick inside and explore life as a 3-technique pass-rushing interior player at the next level.

name: Edge Josh Sweat
overview: Explosive out of his stance. Can press tackles upfield shoulder and get them off balance. Struggles turning the corner. Even when he gets the edge on tackles, he often can’t turn back to the QB. Never truly dominated a game from start to finish. Was held without a pressure in two separate games this past season. Rarely won if it wasn’t on first contact. Lot of pass-rushes with no real plan of attack after the first move. Length to long arm tackles and keep them at bay. Especially shows up in the run game.
bottom_line: Sweat never quite lived up to his recruiting hype at Florida State before de- claring early for the draft. He has the height and length the NFL is looking for, but was limited by a lack of flexibility on the edge. You can’t teach some of the traits he has though and he will draw interest as a project.

name: Edge Chad Thomas
overview: Proficient hands fighter. Powerful first strike when he wants to use it. Average athlete for the edge. First step isn’t going to worry offensive tackles. Struggles cornering. Got pushed past the pocket far more than you’d like against college tackles. Battering ram. Size and strength to rush the passer from the inside as well as outside. Mediocre production for his career. Three-year starter with only 49 total stops over that span. Flashes dominant potential with some incredibly impressive reps.
bottom_line: Thomas is a physical specimen, but didn’t dominate in college like his traits would suggest. That’s always concerning, but he took a big step forward this past year from previous seasons. Thomas has the versatility to play from multi- ple alignments, and should at worst be a plus run defender in the NFL.

name: Edge Kemoko Turay
overview: Bendy big man at 6-foot-5, 252 pounds who has the sort of flexibility that can’t be taught. Athleticism combined with length is a deadly combo as a pass-rusher. Can execute myriad of pass-rushing moves. Won 55 percent of his 1-on-1s at the senior bowl, the 2nd-best rate of any edge there. Limited experience playing the run. Doesn’t have the strength you’d want for a typical edge setter. Had some horrible reps in run defense when offensive tackles got into his pads. Could be designated pass-rusher at next level. Agility to cross face of tackles with ease. Closes to ball carriers and quarterbacks with explosiveness when he gets clean.
bottom_line: Turay is a very interesting evaluation. He was dominant as a designated pass-rusher back in 2014 and 2015 (559 snaps combined). Back then he looked more like a wide receiver though. After putting on weight and getting a more full-time role in 2017, his dominance subsided greatly. With so little informa- tion to go on, his performance at the combine will be enormous for his draft stock.

name: Andrew Brown
overview: Slightly built defensive tackle with little college production to speak of. Would disappear for whole games at a time. 7 sacks in college career. Plays with terrific leverage. Able to consistently move the line of scrimmage when going 1-on-1. Asked to play run first from a frog stance most snaps. Scheme not well suited to his strengths. Getting off of blocks is a major issue. Seemingly attached to offensive linemen far too often. Almost awkward looking in his movements. Nothing looks terribly natural about his play style. Pass-rushing toolbox is incredibly limited at this point. Only 35 pressures all last season. Never truly dominated.
bottom_line: Brown flashed a number of reps that make him an intriguing evaluation, but they were so few and far between that you’re left wanting more. He’s graded out right around average all four seasons in college and isn’t so athletic that makes one think there’s underlying potential he hasn’t reached.

name: Taven Bryan
overview: First step is fantastic. Got plenty of college guards completely off balance with how quickly he got on top of them. Flexibility of a man much smaller than his listed 290-plus pounds. Can dip and rip on guards. Tweener who may ultimately be best suited playing outside the tackles rather than inside. Power in his strike is nothing special. Not the kind of defensive tackle who can stand offensive linemen up on contact. Block awareness was poor in the run game. Would get washed completely out of plays from not seeing where block was coming from. Weapon on stunts with his ability to crash the B-gap.
bottom_line: Bryan has the kind of first step that GMs will fall in love with – especially in a light defensive line class. It’s concerning though that Florida let Bryan explode off the line of scrimmage consistently and he still wasn’t anything special production-wise. He’s a project in a number of ways, but his flashes suggest he could someday put it all together.

name: Poona Ford
overview: Built like an ox. Short for the position but carries 300-plus pounds with ease. Consistently a line of scrimmage mover when going 1-on-1. Takes on blocks with little plan of attack. All too often puts his head down and drives. Nothing as a pass-rusher. Hand usage needs a lot of work. Only 22 total pressures this past season. Often the 0-tech in Texas’ defense. Looked out of place and was far less effective when he didn’t get to simply fire into the center ever snap. Still light as far as nose tackles go and struggled to hold up to double teams.
bottom_line: Ford has a lot of knocks against him. He’s an undersized nose tackle that offers nothing as a pass-rusher. It’s a role that’s simply being phased out of many NFL defenses and will limit him to aggressive, one-gapping teams only. His multi- ple seasons of grading are difficult to overlook though, and he has the build to put on some more weight in time.

name: Will Geary
overview: Listed at 6-0, 306, but could even be shorter than that. Noticeably much lower to the ground in his stance than everyone else. Some of the most active hands in the entire class. He’s not going to quit until he’s shed the block. Poor athlete. No closing speed whatsoever and first step leaves a lot to be desired. Uncanny balance. Will fight through multiple bodies and somehow be upright and ready to make a play still. Holds up to double teams extremely well. Great natural leverage. Has been one of highest graded run defenders for multiple years. Experience playing three technique as well as nose tackle in Kansas State’s defense. Ugly reps when he does lose. When Offensive linemen get in his pads he can get moved easily.
bottom_line: Few defensive linemen in the entire country can match Geary’s production over the course of his college career. His 91.2 overall grade was third-best in the FBS last year as he made huge strides as a pass-rusher. It rarely looks pret- ty, but Geary gets the job done. His lack of height and athleticism leaves him without a true position in the NFL, but I wouldn’t want to bet against him.

name: Da’shawn Hand
overview: A phenomenal looking athlete, saw just 1,014 snaps in his college career after being a star high school recruit. Has been a better run defender than pass-rusher at Alabama, notching a dozen defensive stops in each of the last two years. Had back-to-back dominant games against Colorado State and Vanderbilt in 2017, imposing himself as a run defender. Was almost anonymous in the National Title game against Georgia, notched just a single hit on the quarterback from 56 snaps. Graded well during practices at the Senior Bowl, particularly on inside moves or the bullrush. A player whose draft stock is based almost entirely on potential rather than production.
bottom_line: Hand was once the No. 1 overall high school recruit in the country, but since that point has played very sparingly at Alabama – never more than 43.7 percent of the possible defensive snaps – and has only flashed the elite potential he does possess. Dominated individual games but has never had an extended stretch of excellent play and has been particularly anonymous as a pass-rusher. NFL teams will likely boost him up their boards based on prototypical measurables, but he needs to find consistent play at the next level to be anything more than a rotational body.

name: B.j. Hill
overview: Penetrating defensive end. At his best when he’s allowed to fire off into the backfield. Extremely inconsistent. Would disappear for games at a time. Four games this year without a single pressure. Highest grade, far and away the best performer in Senior Bowl 1-on-1s. Won 73 percent of his reps there. Not much of an anchor against double teams. Lower body strength leaves something to be desired. Versatility to play any alignment between the tackles. Took 84 snaps as a nose tackle last season. Hit and miss with his leverage. Doesn’t fire off particularly low at the snap and can get forklifted by offensive linemen. Creative pass-rusher who times his move well. Killed a ton of guards this year with a spin move.
bottom_line: Hill will be limited by his athleticism at the next level, but can still be a push- the-pocket type of nose tackle. The problem is, he won’t be a run-stuffing nose tackle anytime soon and some teams aren’t ready to make that trade off. His performance at the Senior Bowl practices was hard to ignore and will attract teams looking for some pass-rush from the nose tackle position.

name: Maurice Hurst
overview: Incredibly explosive off the ball. When he fires off as pass-rusher there’s a noticeable difference between him and others in this class. Almost always wins leverage battle. Plays very low even for an undersized DT. Led all DT/NTs with 49 total pressures. Superb motor. Always fighting even when initially stoned as pass-rusher. Will chase from backside of runs and screens. Small strike zone for opposing offensive linemen. Can rarely get him locked up cleanly Holding up to double teams difficult at his size. Played 237 snaps at NT in 2017, but almost has to be 3-tech only in NFL. Awareness can be an issue. Will attack blocks head down and lose ball carriers Balance is iffy at times. Has some ugly reps when he gets off balance and can get swallowed by Offensive linemen.
bottom_line: Hurst is the cream of this defensive tackle crop. There isn’t another interior player that can come close to his production as a pass-rusher in college and everything on tape suggests it will translate to the NFL. His size will give teams pause, but at no point in his college career was it ever a serious issue against the run – he still ranked 14th nationally in run-stop percentage. Hurst is a con- sistently dominant force whose only real question marks have little to do with his on-field performance.

name: Rj Mcintosh
overview: Havoc creator. McIntosh wants to disrupt every single play by fighting his way into the backfield in some way, shape, or form. Legit range in the run game. Can work his way from the backside to the front side and still finish on the ball carrier. Slightly built to translate to the NFL game. Looks more like a defensive end at this point than a 3-tech. Plays higher than you’d like against both run and pass. Form against double teams is non-existent much of the time. Plays neither blocker and can get owned. Led to him getting his butt kicked to his lowest grade all year in the bowl game against Wisconsin. High motor type player who’s will to make plays is inspiring. Not always the most technically sound pass-rusher, but fights snap after snap.
bottom_line: McIntosh is an athletic 3-technique, defensive end tweener that profiles to attacking 1-gap defenses. He’s not so overtly athletic though to where you’d fall in love with him at the top of the draft. Still, McIntosh is one of the few interior players in this class who offers legitimate pass-rushing tools that will translate to the NFL.

name: Derrick Nnadi
overview: Stout frame that’s difficult to out-leverage and generate movement on 1-on-1 and Nnadi knows how to play low. At the same time, Nnadi struggled to consistently move the line of scrimmage the other way in the run game. Impressive mobility for a nose tackle. Centers had a hard time reaching him from a shade. Limited pass-rushing skill-set. Registered all of 19 pressures this season and was shut out in seven different games. Struggled cleanly separating from offensive linemen in the run game. Lack of length could be an issue. Consistently productive. Only one truly poorly graded game in the past three seasons.
bottom_line: Nnadi might look like a pass-rushing 3-technique, but his best position at the next level is likely nose tackle. He simply doesn’t offer enough as a pass-rusher to warrant early consideration, but it’s hard to overlook three straight seasons grading above 82.0 for us. He never quite took the next step after a strong sophomore campaign though, and even took a step backwards as a pass-rusher this year.

name: Kevon Perry
overview: Bully at Louisiana this past season. Manhandled the offensive linemen of the Sun Belt. Was nearly unblockable in the run game at times. Had the 4th most run- stops (32) among interior players. Very little lateral agility. Will limit him as a pass-rusher at the next level. Purely a power player. Terribly unrefined as a pass-rusher. No real moves to speak of outside of barreling into offensive linemen. Size likely limits him to a three-technique at the next level. Still let offensive linemen into his pads too often. Often won after fighting to get himself clean instead of staying clean in the first place.
bottom_line: Perry is one of the most intriguing small school defensive tackles in the draft class. He came out of nowhere to be an absolute force against the run in 2017. Unfortunately, his pass-rush still left a lot to be desired, as he won mainly through a strength advantage that won’t be present in the NFL. That’s not to say he can’t develop, but he’s some ways away from contributing in that regard.

name: Da’ron Payne
overview: As with most defensive linemen from Alabama, very technically sound as a run defender and pass-rusher already. High swipe is his go-to pass-rushing move. Likes to hands fight with opposing offensive linemen. Tackle radius is fantastic – especially if teams see him as a nose tackle. Can make plays up and down the line of scrimmage. Heavy hands. When he wins, it’s usually on first contact where he can control the interaction from the jump. Rarely wow’d as a pass-rusher. Not a ton of clean, quick, dominant wins. Motor is nothing special. Struggled to chase down quarterbacks when moved off their spot. Blew up the national championship game, where he was the highest graded player.
bottom_line: Payne is an NFL ready defensive tackle whose versatility will push him up draft boards. He is comfortable performing in any alignment imaginable between the tackles without his performance declining. At the same time though, he never truly dominated until the Georgia game. He’s not near the pass-rusher that Jonathan Allen was a season ago, but his game should still translate quick- ly to the league.

name: Harrison Phillips
overview: Primarily a nose tackle at Stanford (455 snaps last season), but unlikely to hold up there in the NFL. Very disciplined against the run. Often played head up nose tackle and did well to keep his two-way go versus the center. Much more developed as a run defender than pass-rusher at this point. Didn’t have an above average pass-rushing grade until this season. That being said, was asked to be a run first player much of the time in Stanford’s scheme. Fantastic awareness in the run game. Eyes always tracking running back. Led all defensive tackles this past season with 46 run-stops. Nothing special athletically. Wins almost exclusively with strength and technique. Showed the ability to take over games against Oregon State and USC, with two of the highest graded games this season.
bottom_line: Phillips doesn’t have the sort of raw, physical traits that turns heads, but he does have an impressive track record of performance that’s seen him improve every single year of his career. In a defensive line class lacking high-end talent, Phillips could move up boards because of how capable he is of contributing right away as a run defender.

name: Deadrin Senat
overview: Squatty defensive tackle with thick build throughout. Limited length but shouldn’t be a huge issue at nose tackle. Ability to slide into any alignment between the tackles and not be out of place. Usage of leverage is fantastic. Comes naturally at his height, but he still fires off low. Bench presses centers with his hands above his eyes. Technique versus the run is a plus. Surprisingly not much of a pocket pusher. Got it done more with his hands and athleticism as a pass-rusher but will be limited in that regard at NFL level. Plays with a reckless streak as a pass-rusher. Relishes his chance to take shots at opposing quarterbacks.
bottom_line: Athleticism in a nose tackle is rare, but Senat possesses it. That in and of itself will put him on NFL radars. Add to it the way he plays with leverage and his overall hand usage and you have a mid-round prospect that could make an impact early in his NFL career.

name: Tim Settle
overview: Powerful big man who flashes some of the most impressive reps of the entire class. Rare coordination for a man his size. Balance is a serious issue. Ends up on the ground far too often on seemingly innocuous blocks. Gets playmaking happy at times and can easily get caught out of position. A redshirt sophomore with two seasons of outstanding grading for his age. Has the size of a nose tackle, but the play style of a 3-technique. Could be best served to drop weight in NFL. Shows the ability to separate off blocks consistently and finish plays.
bottom_line: Everyone wants the mythical nose tackle that can also rush the passer and Settle certainly fits that billing. As intriguing as his high-end is, his low-end is equally concerning. He’s terribly unrefined at this point and for all the hype around his athleticism, his disappointing performance at the combine sug- gests he might not have the perceived ‘upside’ some think.

name: Trenton Thompson
overview: Violent hands and first strike. Has the ability to ragdoll and toss aside opposing offensive linemen like it’s nothing. Balance is an issue. Gets top heavy and has trouble staying on his feet when changing directions. Double teams were a problem. Had reps where he got taken out of the play completely. Injuries plagued him throughout his college career. Only played 1,079 snaps his entire college career. Checks boxes from a size and athleticism perspective. Ideal 3-4 defensive end toolbox to take on guards and tackles. Rangy versus the run. Can win quickly and close on the opposite side of the line of scrimmage. Not a power player. Wants to win with quicks and isn’t quick enough to win consistently that way as pass-rusher.
bottom_line: Thompson is a bull in a china shop at this point in his development. His game is unrefined and even awkward looking at times, but it still got the job done. His injuries are a concern, as is his mediocre pass-rushing prowess (only 13 total pressures this year). Thompson is an intriguing player after the top of the crop is gone on the interior.

name: Vita Vea
overview: Rare coordination for a 340-pound man. Dancing bear-esque qualities. Even mixes in a spin move from time-to-time. An absolute unit. Dominated from first snap to the last against the run. Plays with immense power and solid leverage for his size. Tackle radius is iffy at best. More disruptor than finisher. Only 25 run- stops on the year. Was already on a very limited snap count at Washington. Played only 62 percent of their defensive snaps this past season (554 total). Already a well-developed pass-rushing repertoire. Hump was his go-to move, but also push-pulled well. Worrisome that he still ran hot and cold even on limited snap counts. Some low energy reps on film. Three games with only 1 pressure in 2017.
bottom_line: The evaluation of Vea is as much about value as it is about talent. There’s no denying that he could step in and be a force at nose tackle from day one, but how much will he offer as a pass-rusher and how many snaps can he play? He’s only played over 50 percent of his team’s snaps in one season in college. It’s going to be tough to get first-round value if he can only be a two-down player in the NFL.

name: Genard Avery
overview: Played both inside and outside linebacker for Memphis, with 533 of his 884 snaps outside in 2017. Pass-rush has been consistently his best trait, and he notched 57 total pressures in 2017, though was shut out in the NFLPA Bowl. Run defense has also been solid and his run-stop percentage ranked inside the top 20 in the nation in 2017. 50 defensive stops were also good enough to rank top 20 in the nation among all linebackers. Coverage has been his weakness, with poor grades in all but one season. He allowed 11.3 yards per catch over his college career, including 14.4 in 2017, his most extensive playing time in coverage.
bottom_line: Avery needs to be tied down to a position at the NFL level, after he played both inside linebacker and outside, edge rushing linebacker for Memphis. His strength has been pass-rushing to date, with solid run defense, while coverage has been a weakness, so he may naturally project to the edge. His immediate route to NFL playing time may be special teams while teams work out how best to deploy him on defense.

name: Jerome Baker
overview: Graded solidly in 2017, but was dramatically better the season before for the Buckeyes, earning an overall grade of 87.7 as a sophomore. Was at his best in 2017 during the Big-10 Championship game and the team’s bowl game against USC. Allowed three touchdowns in coverage in each of his past two seasons of play, notched just two interceptions and two pass breakups over that span. Has speed to burn and can be extremely effective coming forward towards the line of scrimmage Has the skills to mirror receivers and stick with them in coverage, but needs to improve challenging at the catch point. Is significantly more lost in zone coverage, and will need to improve that at the next level to be a three-down player.
bottom_line: Jerome Baker has the athletic profile of a top pick in this draft, and at least one season of play that suggested he can live up to that potential. Took a step back in 2017, which is always a concern, but has the skills to attack at speed against the run and cover backs and tight ends in man coverage. Will need to develop his game as a zone defender to avoid being a scheme-specific player in the NFL.

name: Ja’whaun Bentley
overview: Hard nosed downhill thumper at linebacker who was PFF’s top graded linebacker in the draft class in 2017 thanks to his run defense. Had 53 defensive stops this season, with 79 solo tackles and 35 assists. Played at the Senior Bowl and struggled in coverage during 1-on-1 drills. Saw just one rep in pass-rush drills but won that rep. Had a relatively anonymous outing in the game itself, posting an average grade and just one tackle from 30 snaps for the North team. Struggles to change direction in space and may be athletically short of the NFL standard to convert his college production to the next level. Shows the ability to play strong in tight spaces, shucking off blocks and forcing cuts from running backs behind the line.
bottom_line: Ja’Whaun Bentley had an exceptional PFF grade this season, which came almost entirely in the run game where he was a consistent hammer. He is no- ticeably stiff in his movements and will struggle to play in space against more fluid athletes, but when he has the opportunity to operate in tight quarters he can deliver hits and work through contact to find the ball carrier and impact the run game. Struggled at the Senior Bowl in coverage and was anonymous in the game, suggesting that a step up in competition and athlete may cause problems.

name: Al-Rasheed Benton
overview: Three seasons of solid play entering the NFL, but his 2017 season went off the rails at midseason and he struggled in his final two games. Appeared at the NFLPA All-Star game, notched 23 snaps on defense but recorded little but a missed tackle for his troubles. Didn’t allow a touchdown in coverage over the past two seasons, but was only targeted 33 times in primary coverage over that time. Notched two interceptions and three pass breakups in 2017 from just 18 targets, allowed a passer rating of 30.3. Ranked 4th in the draft class among linebackers with 65 defensive stops over the season, and flows quickly to the football. Shows impressive instincts against the run or pass, and has the size to play at the next level, but will need to tighten up mistakes. Missed a monstrous 28 tackles in 2017, the most in the nation and three times as many as he missed in 2016.
bottom_line: Al-Rasheed Benton was a talisman for the West Virginia defense even if his college career ended on a disappointing note with back to back ugly games and a bowl defeat for the Mountaineers.
